A NOTE FROM THE PRINCIPAL

For the grown-ups.

Early science is predicting, testing and talking — never a quiz. Every game here asks your child to commit to a guess first, and every miss brings a friendly explanation instead of a penalty. The say-lines are written so YOU can steal them for bath time and walks.

The worksheets are the paper twins — the same experiments with room to predict, circle and draw. Browse the science worksheets and print the adventure your child loved. Playing games never marks a class complete; only real game finishes do, and only for the child chosen in My Classroom.

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SCIENCE, NATURE & DISCOVERY · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Ant — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson turns a pavement ant into a first science project: your child finds the trail, sets a tiny test, and watches a whole team answer the call — patience, prediction and teamwork, all in one crack in the pavement.

What is this?

Ant teamwork means jobs shared out: a scout finds food, leaves a smell trail on the way home, and the rest of the nest follows that scent line until every crumb is carried away.

What does it mean?

No ant is giving orders; each one follows simple rules — follow the smell, pick up a piece, head home. From those small rules comes something big: a line of workers that behaves like one super-organism.

What does the child need to know?

Ants live in nests with a queen and thousands of workers. They lift loads far heavier than their own bodies, and the trails you see are scent roads — if a raindrop washes one away, the line falls apart until it is rebuilt.

Why this matters

Watching ants teaches two science habits at once: look first, touch nothing, and let the evidence answer. It also plants the idea that small animals run on systems — a thought your child will reuse on bees, fish and even people.

What it teaches

Observation skills (watching without disturbing), prediction ("how many will come?"), counting, patience, and early systems thinking — many small workers, one big result.

Words to learn

anttrailteamscentcarrynest

Say this to your child

“"One ant found this food and told the others with a smell line only ants can read. Now the whole team is carrying it home, piece by piece. Watch how they pass each other without bumping — every ant knows its job, and nobody is the boss."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and ask what the child in the picture is watching — and what the ant is carrying. Name the skill: watching a team at work.
  2. Find a real ant line on a pavement, wall or garden path. Hands behind backs: scientists watch, they do not poke.
  3. Set the crumb test: drop one small breadcrumb just off the path of the line and guess how long the first ant takes to find it.
  4. Count together as more ants arrive — first one, then three, then more than your child can count. Ask what told them where to come.
  5. End with the idea: the first scout left a smell road, and every ant that followed read it with feet and feelers. That is how a team talks without a single word.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: who is the child watching, and what is the ant carrying? Is the leaf bigger than the ant itself? Where do you think the ant is taking it? Can you find where the ant line might be going?

Ask your child

"How did the first ant tell its friends about the food?" "What do ants carry food on?" "What happens if you put your finger on their path?" "Who is the boss of the ant team?"

What your child can say or do

"Ants smell with their feet!" (close — the feelers and legs do the reading), "I counted twelve ants!" Your child may march in a line behind a sibling pretending to carry crumbs, or set a crumb test for ants on every walk.

Out in the real world

Ant teams show up everywhere: pavement cracks, picnic blankets, garden walls, the gap under a flowerpot. Once your child knows the trail rule, every walk becomes a chance to spot a team on shift — and to leave them to it.

Try it together

Crumb relay: you are the scout who finds a "crumb" (a block) across the room; your child smells the trail with a nose-wiggle, then the whole family forms a line and passes crumbs hand to hand to the "nest". Racing the clock makes the teamwork visible.

Understanding check

Ask: "How do ants tell each other about food? Who is the boss? What do scientists do first — touch or watch?" Scent trail, no boss, watch first = landed.

Parent tips

Pick slow pavement edges rather than nests — disturbed ants swarm, which frightens small children. If your child wants to "help" the ants, suggest carrying the crumb test to them, not the ants to the crumb: it respects the workers and keeps fingers safe.

This lesson pairs with the Ant flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Science, Nature & Discovery (Class 31).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SCIENCE, NATURE & DISCOVERY · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Bee — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson reframes the bee from something to fear into a worker with a delivery job: your child learns what the bee takes, what it leaves behind, and why the flowers in the garden are quietly saying thank you.

What is this?

Pollination means moving golden pollen dust from flower to flower. Bees do it by accident: they land to sip sweet nectar, pollen sticks to their fuzzy bodies, and some rubs off inside the next blossom.

What does it mean?

The bee wants nectar, not seeds — but the pollen it carries is exactly what flowers need to make seeds and fruit. Two living things helping each other without either one planning it: that is partnership, and it feeds the whole garden.

What does the child need to know?

A bee can visit hundreds of blossoms in a single day. Pollen is a fine yellow dust made inside flowers; fruit — apples, strawberries, tomatoes — only forms after pollen reaches the right place.

Why this matters

Bees connect animals to plants in your child’s head: the apple on the table needed a bee last spring. That link grows respect for small creatures and answers the garden question "why do we never chase bees?" with real science, not just rules.

What it teaches

Careful observation at a distance, cause-and-effect thinking (bee visits, flower makes fruit), emotional learning about creatures that look alarming but mean no harm, and counting practice disguised as flower-watching.

Words to learn

beeflowerpollennectarseedsfruit

Say this to your child

“"The bee is not bothering the flower — it is drinking sweet juice inside it. Look at its legs: golden dust! That dust is called pollen, and when the bee flies to the next flower, some dust falls off. That little dusting is how flowers make seeds and fruit."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: what is the child watching, and what is the bee visiting? Name the job — this bee is a flower helper.
  2. Explain the two-part visit: the bee drinks sweet nectar deep in the flower, and golden pollen dust sticks to its fuzzy body like glitter.
  3. Count bee visits from a distance: pick two or three flowers in a garden or park, stand back, and tally which one the bees like best.
  4. Connect it to food: many fruits in the kitchen — apples, strawberries — grew only because a bee carried pollen last year.
  5. Practise the garden rule together: bees are busy, not mean. We stand still or walk calmly; we never swat or grab.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: what is the bee visiting? What is the child in the picture doing — running or watching? Where do you think the bee will fly next? Can you point to where the flowers are?

Ask your child

"What is the bee drinking inside the flower?" "What sticks to the bee’s fuzzy body?" "What do flowers make after a bee visits?" "What do we do when a bee flies near — wave or stand calm?"

What your child can say or do

"The bee is wearing pollen glitter!" "Do not chase bees — they are busy workers." Your child may count bee visits out loud in the garden, or explain to a worried friend that the bee is "just helping flowers make apples".

Out in the real world

Bee work is on every table: apples, berries, cucumbers and even the seeds inside tomatoes exist because bees moved pollen. The next fruit bowl becomes a review lesson — "which of these did bees help grow?" — and the answer is nearly all of them.

Try it together

Pollen glove game: put a sock or glove on your child’s hand, dust it with flour "pollen", and have them touch five paper flowers around the room. Check each flower afterwards for flour — that is pollination, replayed by hand.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does the bee drink? What sticks to its body? What do flowers make from pollen? What do we do near bees?" Nectar, pollen, seeds and fruit, stay calm = landed.

Parent tips

Watch from a step back rather than leaning in — bees sense sudden movement. Bare feet and flower beds do not mix: bees land on clover low in the grass, which is exactly where bare toes go.

Staying safe

Bees sting only when scared or squeezed — a calm child standing still is safe, and a bee buzzing past is on its way somewhere. If a bee does sting, it hurts honestly and briefly: tell a grown-up, wash the spot, and a cold cloth takes the heat down. A very swollen face or any trouble breathing means a grown-up calls a doctor straight away.

This lesson pairs with the Bee flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Science, Nature & Discovery (Class 31).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SCIENCE, NATURE & DISCOVERY · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Snail — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson makes the slowest animal in the garden the best first subject: a snail moves at exactly the speed a four-year-old studies, and everything about it — shell, slime, feelers — is visible without any chasing.

What is this?

A snail is a soft-bodied animal with a spiral shell it never leaves: the shell is its home, its shield and its bones in one. Underneath, a single muscular foot ripples forward, laying down slippery slime as it goes.

What does it mean?

The shell answers a big question — where does a soft animal keep safe? — by carrying the answer along. The slime is not mess; it is a road, a glue and a drying-guard all at once, which is why a snail can climb a wall or slide under a leaf and stick there.

What does the child need to know?

Snails come out when it is damp — after rain, at dawn, in shady corners — because drying out is their biggest danger. The shell grows with the snail, coil by coil, and the two feelers on top carry tiny eyes at their tips.

Why this matters

Snails reward patience like nothing else in the garden: the child who sits still for two minutes gets a whole show — stretching, gliding, tasting the air. Slow animals teach the watching skills fast animals cannot.

What it teaches

Sustained attention (snails reward stillness), close observation, gentle handling of ideas like protection and shelter, and the patience-muscle that underpins every later science lesson.

Words to learn

snailshellslimeslowfeelersdamp

Say this to your child

“"A snail carries its house everywhere — no other animal does that. When it is scared, it pulls everything inside and shuts the door. Underneath is one strong foot that ripples like a wave, and the slime is its slippery road so the soft parts never get hurt on the ground."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: who is watching whom, and what is the snail wearing on its back? Name the home-carrying trick.
  2. Ask the big question: where does a snail sleep? Answer — inside itself, door closed. The shell is bedroom and shield together.
  3. Hunt after rain: shady grass, damp walls, under pots. Move slowly; slow animals trust slow people.
  4. Follow the shiny trail backwards and ask where the snail came from — slime is a road you can read.
  5. Finish by watching one snail stretch out and glide: two quiet minutes is a long time at four, and a snail makes every second count.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: what shape is the snail’s shell — can you trace the spiral with a finger in the air? What is the child in the picture doing? Where do you think the snail is heading? Can you find anything else in the picture that looks damp?

Ask your child

"Where does a snail keep its house?" "Why do we find snails after rain?" "What is the shiny line on the ground?" "What does a snail do when it is scared?"

What your child can say or do

"The snail took its house inside!" "Look — its slime road goes all the way to the wall!" Your child may crawl slowly around the garden calling themselves a snail, or check the same wall every morning for "their" snail.

Out in the real world

Snail shells show up in stories, spirals and staircases once your child starts looking — the swirl is one of nature’s favourite shapes. Gardeners have a different view of snails: your child now understands both sides, the admirer and the lettuce-farmer.

Try it together

Spiral hunt: draw one big spiral, then find snail-swirl shapes around you — shells, cinnamon rolls, curled fern tips, the coil of a hose. Then slow-race: everyone moves like a snail from sofa to door; last one wins, of course.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does a snail carry on its back? What is the shiny trail for? When do snails come out?" Shell-home, slime-road, after-rain = landed.

Parent tips

If your child wants to hold a snail, wet hands first and keep it low over soft grass — a dropped shell cracks. Always put the snail back exactly where it was found; its whole world is that one damp corner.

This lesson pairs with the Snail flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Science, Nature & Discovery (Class 31).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SCIENCE, NATURE & DISCOVERY · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Spider — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson turns spider webs from spooky into clever: a net designed by an animal, strung between plants, that catches the spider’s dinner without one single chase. Fear shrinks fast when engineering takes its place.

What is this?

A spider web is a net made of silk — a thread the spider’s own body spins. The sticky spirals catch flying insects; the spider feels the shake through its legs and knows dinner has landed.

What does it mean?

The web is the spider’s fishing net and dinner bell at once: it catches food AND rings the news. Silk comes from the spider’s own body, thread by thread, which makes a web one of the few tools an animal builds from itself.

What does the child need to know?

Spiders have eight legs, so they are arachnids — not insects, which have six. Silk is astonishingly strong for its weight, and some spiders rebuild the whole trap daily — eating the old one first to recycle the material.

Why this matters

Webs make engineering visible: spokes, frame, spiral — a child can see the design. Learning that spiders eat pests (flies, mosquitoes) flips the fear script: the web is a helpful trap, and the spider is night-shift pest control.

What it teaches

Respectful distance from small creatures, design thinking (parts with jobs: frame, spokes, trap), the insect-versus-arachnid sorting idea, and courage that grows from understanding rather than avoidance.

Words to learn

spiderwebsilklegsstickycatch

Say this to your child

“"A spider makes its own thread — real silk, from its own body. It builds the spokes first, then a spiral sticky enough that flying insects get stuck. When something lands, the web shakes like a doorbell, and the spider comes out to collect its dinner."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: who is sitting in the middle of the net, and what is the child looking at? Count the spider’s legs together — how many?
  2. Explain the plan of a web: strong spokes first, like a bicycle wheel, then the sticky spiral wound round and round.
  3. Hunt for a web in the early morning or after rain, when dew drops make every thread shine. Look with eyes only — the web took hours to build.
  4. Sort it out loud: spiders have eight legs, flies and bees six. Eight means arachnid, and arachnids spin silk.
  5. Close with the good-deed idea: the fly a web catches is one less fly in the kitchen. The spider is the garden’s quiet cleaner.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: where is the spider sitting? What is the child in the picture doing — touching the web or looking? Can you see the lines of the web crossing like a wheel? How many legs can you count on the spider?

Ask your child

"What is a web made of?" "How many legs does a spider have?" "What happens when a fly lands in the web?" "Are we allowed to touch a web? Why not?"

What your child can say or do

"The web is the spider’s dinner bell!" "Eight legs — arachnid, not insect!" Your child may hunt for webs every dewy morning, or gently warn guests that the garden web took the spider all night to build, so hands off.

Out in the real world

Webs appear where food flies: window corners, garden gates, hedge gaps, bicycle frames left overnight. Once your child can name the wheel pattern, a walk becomes a web safari — and empty webs are evidence the builder is nearby.

Try it together

Be the spider: tape or string a "web" between chair legs, then throw paper-fly balls at it — which stick, which fall through? The sticky-zone idea lands hard. Then your child repairs the broken web with new string, feeling how fiddly silk work is.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do spiders build webs from? How many legs? What happens when food lands?" Silk, eight, the web shakes and the spider comes = landed.

Parent tips

Dew or drizzle is the web-hunter’s friend; midday sun hides the threads. If a web is built across a doorframe, leave it one day and watch the spider repair it — better than any worksheet on engineering.

This lesson pairs with the Spider flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Science, Nature & Discovery (Class 31).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SCIENCE, NATURE & DISCOVERY · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Butterfly Begins as a Caterpillar — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the butterfly story at the beginning — a tiny egg on a leaf hatches into a hungry crawler — and gives your child the garden habit that matters: find a caterpillar, look closely, and leave it to its lunch.

What is this?

A caterpillar is a butterfly’s baby stage: it hatches from an egg laid on a leaf and spends its days eating leaves and growing, shedding its tight skin several times before it is ready for the next stage.

What does it mean?

The caterpillar’s whole job is one word: grow. Every bite is stored for the big change ahead. That is why it never stops munching — it is a living lunchbox, packing away fuel for wings it does not have yet.

What does the child need to know?

Butterfly mothers lay eggs on the exact leaves their babies can eat. A caterpillar’s body is soft with rings called segments, and it grows so fast it must crawl out of its own skin again and again.

Why this matters

Knowing what caterpillars are DOING on leaves changes how a child treats them: not a toy to grab but a worker on a deadline. It also sets up the life-cycle idea — this card is chapter one of a story your child will meet again.

What it teaches

Gentle observation, impulse control (look, do not grab), the idea that animals have jobs at each stage of life, and story-sequencing instincts — beginnings, middles and endings.

Words to learn

caterpillarleafeggeatgrowbutterfly

Say this to your child

“"Every butterfly was a caterpillar first. The mother laid her egg on just the right leaf, and the baby’s job is simple: eat leaves, grow bigger, shed your skin when it gets tight. All that food is being packed away for the wings it will grow later."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: what is resting beside the leaf, and what is the child watching? Name both — butterfly AND caterpillar — and ask how they could be connected.
  2. Tell the beginning: a butterfly laid a tiny egg on a leaf, and out crawled this caterpillar. Chapter one of a story.
  3. Explain the job: caterpillars eat and eat and eat — leaves are their only food, and growing is their only work.
  4. Hunt gently: look along and under garden leaves for nibbled holes and slow crawlers. Found one? Count its body rings, watch it munch if you are lucky — then leave it exactly there.
  5. End with the promise: this crawler is packing away fuel for wings. Chapter two comes next lesson.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: what is the child in the picture watching? Can you find the caterpillar AND the butterfly? Which one has wings? Which one has more legs? Where do you think the caterpillar is hiding on the leaf?

Ask your child

"What was the butterfly before it had wings?" "What does a caterpillar eat all day?" "Why does the mother lay her egg on a leaf?" "What should we do if we find a caterpillar?"

What your child can say or do

"Caterpillars eat and eat and eat!" "Do not grab it — it is growing!" Your child may check the same leaves on every garden walk, or retell the story backwards: "the butterfly’s mummy was an egg, no wait — the egg was the butterfly’s beginning!"

Out in the real world

Cabbage patches, nettles and hedge rows are caterpillar nurseries once you know to look for nibbled edges — those holes are breakfast evidence. Farmers know it too: caterpillars eat crops, birds eat caterpillars, and the garden keeps its balance.

Try it together

Munch game: cut a big green paper leaf, give your child a hole punch, and let them "eat" it like a caterpillar — punch, punch, punch. Then measure: how many punches until the caterpillar is full? Body-ring craft follows with a painted egg box.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is a caterpillar’s job? What does it eat? What do we do when we find one?" Eat-and-grow, leaves, look-and-leave = landed.

Parent tips

Caterpillar hunting teaches more with a rule of two hands behind the back — eyes do the touching. If your child begs to keep one, a leaf from the same plant in a jar with air holes is a short, honest visit; release it the same day.

This lesson pairs with the Butterfly Begins as a Caterpillar flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Science, Nature & Discovery (Class 31).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SCIENCE, NATURE & DISCOVERY · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Butterfly Life Cycle — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson takes the whole journey at once — egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, butterfly — and teaches it as a four-chapter story your child can sequence, draw and retell, ending with the word that names the magic: metamorphosis.

What is this?

A butterfly changes form four times in one life: egg, then caterpillar, then chrysalis, then winged adult. Inside the chrysalis, the old caterpillar body dissolves and rebuilds as something with wings.

What does it mean?

Metamorphosis means "changing shape" — and the chrysalis is where the quiet work happens: nothing is wasted, the old body is rearranged into a new one. Change in nature is not instant; it is staged, and every stage has a job.

What does the child need to know?

The chrysalis looks still but is working hard inside — scientists who peeked found the caterpillar turns almost to liquid before rebuilding. A hatched butterfly’s wings start crumpled and must fill and dry before the first flight.

Why this matters

This is the most dramatic change your child can actually find in a garden, which makes it the perfect first life cycle. Sequencing the four stages builds ordering skills, and the story carries a quiet message: big change is natural, and slow stages count too.

What it teaches

Sequencing and retelling (four chapters in order), vocabulary building (a real science word), comfort with transformation stories — tadpoles and seeds will reuse the pattern — and drawing as a thinking tool.

Words to learn

eggcaterpillarchrysalisbutterflychangewings

Say this to your child

“"A butterfly has four chapters. Egg, tiny and round on a leaf. Caterpillar, eating everything. Chrysalis, hanging like a sleeping bag while its body rebuilds inside. Then butterfly — new wings, new life. The word for that big change is metamorphosis."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and hunt the three characters on the leaf: caterpillar, chrysalis, butterfly. Which one is missing from the picture? The egg — that is chapter one.
  2. Walk the story with one finger: first the egg on the leaf, then the munching caterpillar, then the quiet chrysalis, then the wings.
  3. Tell the chrysalis secret: it looks like nothing is happening, but inside, the caterpillar is rebuilding its whole body into a butterfly.
  4. Draw the wheel: four circles on paper, one for each stage — your child fills them and then retells the story round and round.
  5. Learn the big word: metamorphosis. Clap it out — me-ta-mor-fo-sis — and let your child own it.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: how many stages can you find on the leaf in the picture? Which stage is the caterpillar, and which is the chrysalis? Does the butterfly look new or old? What is the child watching for?

Ask your child

"What are the four stages, in order?" "What happens inside the chrysalis?" "What is the big word for changing shape?" "Which stage do you think takes longest?"

What your child can say or do

"Me-ta-mor-fo-sis!" — said at full volume, often. "The chrysalis is a sleeping bag, not a shell." Your child may line up four toys to show the four stages, or retell the wheel starting anywhere and insist it still works.

Out in the real world

The pattern repeats all over nature once your child knows to look: tadpoles become frogs, seeds become plants, and mealworms in a pet shop turn into beetles. Same shape of story — start small, change completely — in garden after garden.

Try it together

Stage race: four corners of the room — egg (curled tiny), caterpillar (wriggle-crawl), chrysalis (stand still, arms wrapped), butterfly (flap and fly). Call the stages in any order and let your child transform on the spot. Then backwards!

Understanding check

Ask: "Name the four stages in order. What happens inside the chrysalis? What is metamorphosis?" Egg-caterpillar-chrysalis-butterfly, rebuilding, change = landed.

Parent tips

Let your child draw the wheel BEFORE hearing the story and guess what happens between stages — the wrong guesses ("the caterpillar takes a nap") make the truth land harder. Go chrysalis-hunting under leaves and along fence rails; they hide in plain sight, looking like tiny dried leaves.

This lesson pairs with the Butterfly Life Cycle flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Science, Nature & Discovery (Class 31).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SCIENCE, NATURE & DISCOVERY · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Frog — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson follows the second great change-your-body story in the garden: the frog. Your child learns that pond animals start as swimmers, watches what legs are for, and practises the pondside habit of looking without scooping.

What is this?

A frog starts life as an egg in a blob of jelly, hatches as a tadpole that swims and breathes underwater, then slowly grows four legs, loses its tail and hops out onto land as a breathing, jumping frog.

What does it mean?

The tadpole is not a different animal from the frog — it is the same frog at a different age, built for a different home. First a water body with a tail and gills, then a land body with legs and lungs: one life, two designs.

What does the child need to know?

Tadpoles hatch in spring from frogspawn — soft jelly dots laid on pond plants. As a tadpole grows, its tail gets shorter until it disappears, and lungs take over from gills. Frogs breathe a little through their skin too, and they hop instead of walk.

Why this matters

Frogs give your child a second life-cycle after the butterfly, and this one happens in a place they can visit: a pond. Matching bodies to homes — tail for swimming, legs for hopping — is the first step toward understanding habitats.

What it teaches

Sequencing a life story in order, comparing bodies across stages, the habitat idea (water animal, land animal), and gentle pondside discipline: watching without dipping hands or nets into the water.

Words to learn

frogtadpoletaillegspondjump

Say this to your child

“"A baby frog cannot hop at first — it swims! It hatches from a jelly egg as a tadpole, with a long tail for paddling. Little by little it grows legs, the tail disappears, and one day it climbs out of the water and jumps. Same frog, brand-new body."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: who is watching whom, and where is the frog sitting? Name the animal and its home.
  2. Tell the beginning: a frog starts as a jelly dot in the pond, then wiggles out as a tadpole — a tiny swimmer with a tail and no legs.
  3. Walk the change: back legs sprout first, then front legs, then the tail shrinks away while lungs grow for breathing air.
  4. Ask what legs can do that a tail cannot — then hop like frogs across the room, crouch and jump, crouch and jump.
  5. Close with the pond rule: frogspawn and tadpoles stay in their pond — we look, we count, and we leave them to grow.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: who is the child watching? Where is the frog sitting — can you find the lily pad? What is the frog doing? Is the child close to the water or keeping a little distance?

Ask your child

"What does a baby frog look like before it has legs?" "What happens to the tadpole’s tail?" "Why does a frog need legs?" "What do we do at a pond — scoop or watch?"

What your child can say or do

"The tadpole sucked its tail back in!" "Frogs drink through their skin — that is so weird!" (true, and your child said it first). Your child may frog-hop everywhere for a week, or report every spring that the pond frogs will be laying jelly eggs again.

Out in the real world

Frogs turn up wherever water sits still long enough: garden ponds, ditches, rain barrels. Once your child knows the tadpole story, a spring pond visit becomes a scavenger hunt — jelly eggs one week, wiggling tadpoles the next, tiny froglets by summer.

Try it together

Tadpole-to-frog transformation race: start curled small like an egg, wiggle-swim across the rug, grow "legs" (arms out), then hop the last stretch to a lily pad cushion. Call out the stages and let your child transform on command.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does a tadpole use to swim? What grows for hopping? What do we do at the pond?" Tail, legs, watch-only = landed.

Parent tips

Pond dipping needs grown-up hands in charge; bring a white tub to scoop-and-release only where the site allows it, and return every creature straight away. A good pond book or zoomed-in photos stretch the lesson on rainy days.

Staying safe

Ponds earn real respect: little scientists stay a grown-up arm’s length from the water, sit down to watch, and frogspawn or tadpoles never come home — they are living animals, not souvenirs. Nets and buckets only when a grown-up runs the dipping.

This lesson pairs with the Frog flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Science, Nature & Discovery (Class 31).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SCIENCE, NATURE & DISCOVERY · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Fish — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson answers the question every child asks at the fish tank — how on earth does it breathe down there? — and turns a goldfish bowl into a breathing laboratory your child can count, compare and imitate.

What is this?

A fish breathes with gills: water goes in the mouth, pours over the gills hidden behind the gill covers, and the gills snatch the oxygen out of the water — so a fish never has to surface for air the way we do.

What does it mean?

We solve the breathing problem with lungs that take air from the sky; fish solve it with gills that take air from the water. Same job, different tools — comparing solutions is what scientists do all their lives.

What does the child need to know?

Fish never stop pumping: the gill covers flap open and shut like tiny doors, all day and night. Fins steer and brake, the flat tail is the engine, and most fish rest without ever closing their eyes — they have no eyelids to close.

Why this matters

Gills open up the compare-and-contrast habit: fish, frogs and people all need oxygen, but each body finds it somewhere different. Your child also learns to read animal bodies as equipment — every part has a job.

What it teaches

Observation of small repeated movements (gill beats), counting practice, comparison across animals (gills versus lungs), and the deep idea that bodies are built to match where they live.

Words to learn

fishgillswaterbreathefinstail

Say this to your child

“"A fish carries its own breathing gear inside its head. It takes a big sip of water, and while the water pours out over its gills, the gills grab the air out of it. Those flaps opening and closing are the fish breathing — it never has to come up for air."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: what is the child peering at, and where does the goldfish live? Name the bowl and the fish.
  2. Ask the big question: our lungs grab air out of the sky — how does a fish grab air out of the water? Let guesses fly before you answer.
  3. Explain the gill doors: water swims in the mouth, washes over the gills, and the gills grab the air hidden in the water.
  4. Watch a real fish if you can — a bowl, a tank, an aquarium — and count gill beats together for ten seconds.
  5. Compare: you breathe about twenty times a minute at rest; was the fish faster or slower? Finish with fins for steering and the tail for pushing.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: what is the child peering at? Can you find the goldfish? Is the fish swimming in a bowl or the sea? What do you think the fish is looking at?

Ask your child

"What does a fish use to breathe?" "Do fish breathe air or water?" "What do fins do — and the tail?" "How long can you hold your breath under water?"

What your child can say or do

"Gills are doors that grab air!" Your child may puff cheeks and pretend to be a fish, flap hands by their neck like gills, or count the gill beats of every fish they ever meet — bowls, aquariums, and the fish counter at the market.

Out in the real world

Fish live in every patch of water bigger than a bucket: bowls, tanks, garden ponds, rivers, the sea. Once gills make sense, the aquarium becomes a breathing lesson on repeat — and your child knows why a fish out of water flops: its gear only works wet.

Try it together

Gill-breathing pretend: scoop "water" with big armfuls, clap hands to your neck and whisper "grab!" each time — once, twice, all day long. Then switch: you are the fish, your child counts your gill beats, and you race to twenty.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does a fish breathe with? What do gills grab from the water? What pushes a fish along?" Gills, oxygen, the tail = landed.

Parent tips

A home goldfish bowl is a live experiment: one quiet minute of sitting still, and the gill counting works best when nobody taps the glass. Feeding time is bonus science — fish rush the surface, then settle back into their gill rhythm.

This lesson pairs with the Fish flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Science, Nature & Discovery (Class 31).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SCIENCE, NATURE & DISCOVERY · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Bones — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson makes the invisible inside visible: your child presses, bends and wiggles their way to discovering the frame under their skin — and learns that the same quiet scaffolding is busy making blood all day long.

What is this?

Bones are the hard parts inside your body: 206 of them in a grown-up, joined at joints. The skeleton holds you upright, guards the soft organs, gives muscles something to pull on — and the biggest bones are blood factories.

What does it mean?

A body without bones would be a puddle: bones are why you stand, sit, jump and carry. Joints are where the design gets clever — the elbow bends one way, the shoulder swings a circle, and every bend has a limit that keeps it safe.

What does the child need to know?

A baby starts with about 300 soft bones; as you grow, some join together, leaving 206. Bones grow with you — the skeleton of a four-year-old is halfway to its final size. Blood cells are made deep inside the biggest bones, like a factory under the floor.

Why this matters

Feeling your own skeleton turns "bones" from a Halloween word into a body fact. It builds self-knowledge, safety sense (helmets and elbows exist because bones can break), and the habit of asking what is inside things.

What it teaches

Body awareness and self-care vocabulary, sorting (bendy joints versus straight bones), counting to five on the touch hunt, and early engineering thinking: frames, supports and joints, just like a crane or a doll’s stand.

Words to learn

bonesskeletonjointsbendribsskull

Say this to your child

“"Under your skin there is a whole frame, like the poles inside a tent. Bones hold you up, protect the soft parts, and make your blood inside the big ones. Feel that hard ridge in your shin — that is your skeleton, saying hello from inside."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: who is standing beside the child, and does the skeleton look friendly? Wave to the skeleton together.
  2. Start the feel-hunt: press gently on the shin — that hard bit is a bone saying hello. Find the ribs, the elbow, the knee, the skull.
  3. Bend test: wiggle fingers, bend the elbow, swing a shoulder — bones are straight but joints are the bendy hinges between them.
  4. Tell the factory secret: inside the biggest bones, blood is being made all day, every day, without a break.
  5. Count up: a baby starts with about 300 bones, and some join together as you grow — a grown-up has 206. Your child is a building site, in the best way.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: who is standing next to the child in the picture? Does the skeleton look friendly or grumpy? Can you find the skeleton’s ribs? Where are your own ribs right now?

Ask your child

"What do bones do for your body?" "Where do two bones meet?" "What is made inside your biggest bones?" "Why does a baby have more bones than you?"

What your child can say or do

"I can feel my skeleton — it is everywhere!" "Bones make my blood!" Your child may press knuckles to find hard bits all day, count the bones in one hand, or explain that babies have "more bones but smaller ones, and some zip together".

Out in the real world

Skeletons are hiding in every meal and playtime: chicken bones on a plate, the hard knobs of your ankles on stairs, X-ray pictures at the doctor. Once your child can find five bones, every bump and bend becomes a map of the frame inside.

Try it together

Skeleton dance: call out a bone — "ribs!", "skull!", "shin!" — and your child pats it fast, then freezes like a statue. Slow-mo round next: every move in slow motion, feeling which parts bend at joints and which stay straight.

Understanding check

Ask: "What holds your body up? Where do bones bend? What is made inside big bones?" Skeleton, joints, blood = landed.

Parent tips

Keep the touch hunt gentle — bones to find, not bones to bang. If a cast or an X-ray shows up in your family or a friend, bring it out: a real broken-bone story teaches more about why bones matter than any diagram.

This lesson pairs with the Bones flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Science, Nature & Discovery (Class 31).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SCIENCE, NATURE & DISCOVERY · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Eyes — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson treats sight as the superpower it is: your child learns what eyes actually catch, plays the blink game, then switches senses off and on — and discovers that closing the eyes turns the volume up on everything else.

What is this?

Eyes are light catchers: light bounces off everything around you, and the front of your eye gathers it in like a little window, turning the bouncing light into a picture your brain can read. Eyelids blink to wash and protect, and the pair team up on every image.

What does it mean?

Sight is your child’s busiest sense, and it runs on teamwork: two eyes, each catching a slightly different picture, and the brain merging them into one. Blinking is maintenance — thousands of tiny window-wipes a day, mostly without you noticing.

What does the child need to know?

You blink about fifteen times a minute — that adds up to thousands of washes a day. Tears are the eye-cleaning crew, called out for dust or big feelings. Eyes need sleep, hate pokes, and if the world goes blurry, a grown-up and an eye doctor should hear about it.

Why this matters

Knowing how eyes work makes the other senses louder: shut the eyes and hearing, touch and smell step forward. It also plants eye-care habits — no rubbing with dirty hands, reporting blurry vision — through science, not just rules.

What it teaches

Sensory awareness (sight versus hearing), self-care routines, the teamwork idea (two eyes, one picture), and gentle experiment discipline: trying not to blink, timing, and noticing what changes when one sense closes.

Words to learn

eyesseeblinklighteyelidstears

Say this to your child

“"Your eyes are little light catchers. Light bounces off everything and jumps into your eyes, and your brain turns it into pictures — that is seeing. Every blink is a tiny wipe to keep the window clean, and both eyes work together like two cameras making one film."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: what tool is the child holding up, and what is it pointed at? Name it — a magnifying glass, and an enormous eye.
  2. Explain the catching: light bounces off everything — your toy, the table, your face — and your eyes catch the bounce and turn it into pictures.
  3. Play blink-count: try not to blink for as long as you can (it is hard!), then blink fast ten times. That wetting is each blink’s job.
  4. Switch senses: close the eyes for ten seconds and listen. What got louder? The ears take over when the eyes clock off.
  5. End with care: eyes sleep, eyes wash themselves with tears, and pokes or blur mean a grown-up needs to know.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: what is the child holding up? What is the magnifying glass pointed at? How big does the eye look — bigger than a fist? Is the eye looking back at you?

Ask your child

"What do your eyes catch to make pictures?" "Why do we blink?" "What got louder when you closed your eyes?" "What should we do if things look blurry?"

What your child can say or do

"I blinked two hundred times today!" (close — thousands). "My ears got louder when my eyes went to sleep!" Your child may play eyes-closed detective around the house, or report every blink as a "window wash" for a week.

Out in the real world

Eyes work everywhere light works: reading pictures, catching a ball, spotting a ladybird on a leaf. Dim rooms show the limits — eyes need light to catch — and sunglasses on a bright beach, washed hands away from eyes, and good sleep are the care package in action.

Try it together

Ears-only safari: your child closes their eyes while you move around the room making small sounds — keys, a page, a whisper — and they point to where each sound came from. Then swap roles. Closing the eyes is how the other senses get their turn to shine.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do eyes catch to make pictures? What does a blink do? Which sense gets louder with eyes closed?" Light, washing, hearing = landed.

Parent tips

Keep the eyes-closed games short and willing — three to ten seconds feels like a long time at four. If your child squints at books or sits very close to screens, mention it to a grown-up eye doctor; catching it early is the whole game.

This lesson pairs with the Eyes flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Science, Nature & Discovery (Class 31).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SCIENCE, NATURE & DISCOVERY · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Heart — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson makes the busiest organ in the body audible: ten jumps, a palm on the chest, and your child can feel their own engine speed up — then learn what the thump-thump is actually delivering, and to whom.

What is this?

The heart is a muscle that squeezes again and again, pushing blood all around the body. Blood is the delivery crew: it carries oxygen and food to working muscles and picks up what they are done with, and the heartbeat is the sound of that pump at work.

What does it mean?

Move fast and your muscles shout for more oxygen, so the heart pumps faster to keep up — that is why running makes your chest drum. Rest, and the beat settles down. The heart is answering demand, all day, every day, no weekends.

What does the child need to know?

Your heart is about as big as your fist and beats roughly a hundred thousand times a day. Exercise trains it — a well-run heart is strong at pushing. A toy stethoscope, or a grown-up’s ear pressed to the chest, hears the pump directly.

Why this matters

Feeling the heartbeat links exercise to the body’s answer, which is the first cause-and-effect your child can hear with their own hand. It also builds the lifelong idea that moving your body is how you train it — hearts love to be asked to work.

What it teaches

Body awareness, cause-and-effect reasoning (run, then faster beat), measuring by feel (fast, faster, resting), and turn-taking games that end in stillness — the rest-and-listen part is half the lesson.

Words to learn

heartbloodpumpbeatfastrest

Say this to your child

“"Your heart is a pump hidden in your chest. Every squeeze pushes blood out on a delivery run — carrying air and food to your toes, your fingers, your brain. When you jump, your muscles ask for more, so the pump speeds up. That drumming you feel? Your engine, working hard."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: what is the child listening to, and what are they holding to their ears? Name the tool — a stethoscope.
  2. Feel it first: hand flat on the chest, find the thump-thump. That is the heart, pumping right now.
  3. Run the experiment: jump ten times, hand on chest, feel again — faster! Rest until the beat calms, jump again, compare the two.
  4. Explain the deliveries: blood is the van that hauls air and food out to your toes, your fingers, your brain — and the heart is the engine driving it round.
  5. Close with the fist: a heart is about fist-sized, and it squeezes day and night — every thump is one delivery run.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: what is the child listening to? What are they holding against their ears? What color is the heart? Can you point to where your own heart is hiding?

Ask your child

"What does the heart push around your body?" "What happens to your heartbeat when you run?" "What makes the beat slow down again?" "How big is your heart?"

What your child can say or do

"My heart goes fast-fast-fast when I jump!" "It slowed down — my engine is resting." Your child may demand jump-and-listen rounds every evening, press a toy stethoscope to everyone’s chest, or announce "my heart is delivering!" on the stairs.

Out in the real world

Hearts speed up for stairs, dancing, giggling fits and big feelings — your child now has a name for that drumming chest. Calm-down moments get scientific too: slow breaths, a quiet cuddle, and feeling the beat settle are the rest half of the experiment.

Try it together

Heartbeat drums: pat your own chest to your heart’s rhythm while your child copies, then jump ten times together and drum fast. End with a slow-lion-breath round until both drums rest. Loud, fast, slow, quiet — the whole lesson played on your own chest.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does the heart pump? Why does it beat faster when you run? What is blood carrying?" Blood, more oxygen asked for, air and food = landed.

Parent tips

A real stethoscope or a cheap toy one turns this into a favourite toy for weeks — listen to hearts, but also to tummy rumbles and breathing. If your child feels fluttery heartbeats when scared, the science helps: that is the pump getting ready, not a problem.

This lesson pairs with the Heart flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Science, Nature & Discovery (Class 31).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SCIENCE, NATURE & DISCOVERY · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Teeth — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson turns the dinner table into a tool bench: your child discovers which teeth slice, which tear and which grind — and why tools that work all day deserve a proper wash, twice a day, back teeth included.

What is this?

Teeth are food tools in three shapes: flat front teeth slice off bites, pointy side teeth tear tougher food, and wide back teeth grind everything to a mash your tummy can handle. Brushing and spit keep the tools clean between jobs.

What does it mean?

Different shapes do different jobs — the same idea that sorts scissors from saws from spoons. Your child can feel it at every meal: the apple-slice crunch at the front, the big grinding work at the back where nobody can see.

What does the child need to know?

You grow just two sets of teeth in one life: the baby set now, and a hidden grown-up set waiting in the jaw like seeds under soil. Wobbly teeth are normal — the baby tooth is making room. The back grinders matter most and hide from brushes, so they need the longest scrub.

Why this matters

Tooth science makes brushing meaningful instead of a rule from the sky: the tools need cleaning because food sticks to them. Knowing the three jobs also turns eating into an experiment — which teeth am I using right now? — that plays out at every single meal.

What it teaches

Sorting by shape and job, body-part vocabulary, the two-sets idea (a first version of life stages), and habit-building: brushing becomes tool maintenance, with the hidden back teeth as the priority target.

Words to learn

teethbitechewbrushfrontgrind

Say this to your child

“"Your mouth is a toolbox. The flat ones at the front slice like little knives, the pointy ones at the sides tear, and the wide ones at the back grind everything small. Tools that work all day need a wash — that is why we brush, especially the shy grinders hiding at the back."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: what is the child doing, and how big are those teeth? Is the brushing child smiling? Name the job — tool washing.
  2. Set the mirror mission: bite like a rabbit with the front teeth — feel them slicing? Then chew like a lion at the back — feel the grinding?
  3. Sort dinner out loud: bread sliced by the front, chicken torn by the pointy ones, rice ground by the big back teeth.
  4. Count in the mirror: how many teeth can you see? Then hunt the sneaky back ones — the grinders hide from brushes, so they get the longest scrub.
  5. Tell the secret: a second set of grown-up teeth waits in the jaw below, and these baby teeth are the first team — keep them clean so they hand over well.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: what is the child doing? Are the teeth being brushed big or small? Is the child smiling while brushing? Where are your own back teeth hiding right now?

Ask your child

"Which teeth slice off a bite of apple?" "What do the wide back teeth do?" "Why do teeth need brushing?" "What is waiting under your baby teeth?"

What your child can say or do

"I am grinding like a horse!" "The back teeth are hiding from the brush — I got them!" Your child may bite apples only with the front teeth for a while, narrate every meal by tooth job, or announce that the tooth brush is a "tool wash".

Out in the real world

Every meal is a tooth lesson: sandwiches sliced, pizza torn, apples crunched at the front. Dentist visits upgrade the science — the mirror, the counted teeth, the polishing — and a lost first tooth becomes the proudest show-and-tell of the year.

Try it together

Tool tester dinner: serve three foods — something to slice (apple), something to tear (bread roll), something to grind (rice) — and let your child announce which teeth take each job. Brush a big paper tooth afterwards with a dry brush to finish the maintenance story.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do front teeth do? What do back teeth do? Why do we brush?" Slice, grind, wash the tools = landed.

Parent tips

Two-minute brushing works best with a song or a mirror — the back teeth are the slow zone, so park there. If a tooth goes wobbly, celebrate early: a child who knows the two-sets story treats the wiggle as news, not a worry.

This lesson pairs with the Teeth flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Science, Nature & Discovery (Class 31).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SCIENCE, NATURE & DISCOVERY · AGES 4–5 YEARS

What Plants Need — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson sets up the classic first experiment in all of science: grow two plants the same, take something away from one, and watch. Your child learns the three plant needs — and how to test fairly by changing only one thing.

What is this?

Plants run on three things: water sipped up by the roots, light caught by the leaves to cook food, and soil to anchor in and feed from. Miss one out and the plant tells you — drooping, pale or stalling.

What does it mean?

The leaves are the kitchen, the roots are the straws, the soil is the pantry and the anchor. A plant cannot walk to its dinner — it builds its food from light, water and air right where it stands, which is why taking any ingredient away shows fast.

What does the child need to know?

A plant left in darkness turns pale and leggy, stretching after light it cannot find. Roots drink even when the leaves look dry, and overwatering drowns them — plants can have too much of a good thing. Different plants like different amounts.

Why this matters

This is where fair testing begins: two jars, watered the same, one in the light and one in the dark — change one thing, watch, conclude. Your child meets the controlled experiment in bean form, and it will carry through every science lesson after.

What it teaches

Fair-test thinking (change one thing), daily observation and comparison, responsibility through watering routines, and vocabulary for plant parts that recurs through seed, tree and garden lessons.

Words to learn

plantwaterlightsoilrootsleaves

Say this to your child

“"A plant is stuck in one spot, so it carries everything it needs around with it: roots that sip water from the soil, and leaves that catch sunlight and cook it into plant food. Take away one ingredient and the whole machine slows down — that is what our dark-cupboard bean is showing us."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: what is the child giving the seedling? Can you find the roots down in the soil? Name the three needs — water, light, soil.
  2. Ask the detective question: what would a plant do with no water? With no light? With no soil? Collect predictions before testing.
  3. Plant the test: two bean jars on the windowsill, watered the same — then one jar goes into a dark cupboard. Only ONE thing changed.
  4. Check daily: both jars get water, but only one gets light. Which bean is green and sturdy, which is pale and stretchy?
  5. Let your child deliver the verdict: plants need light. Then run it again with water withheld if they are hooked — scientists love a repeat.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: what is the child giving the seedling? Is the seedling big like a tree or small? Can you find where the roots go? What is the seedling growing in?

Ask your child

"What are the three things a plant needs?" "Which part of the plant drinks?" "What do leaves catch to cook plant food?" "What did our dark-cupboard bean tell us?"

What your child can say or do

"The cupboard bean went pale because it was hungry for light!" "Leaves are the kitchen and roots are the straws." Your child may appoint themselves head waterer, check the two jars before breakfast, or explain at a garden centre why the shaded shelf plants look stretchy.

Out in the real world

Plant needs are visible in every home and street: the drooping pot everyone forgot, the leaning office plant chasing the window, the brown patch where the trampoline shaded the grass. Once your child knows the three needs, wilting becomes a clue, not a mystery.

Try it together

Three-needs sorting game: draw or place three picture cards — water, light, soil — and take turns naming a plant (cactus! water lily! oak tree!) while your child points to what that plant loves most. Then water a real plant together, slowly, at the roots.

Understanding check

Ask: "What three things does a plant need? Which part drinks? What did we change in our bean test?" Water-light-soil, roots, the light = landed.

Parent tips

Bean jars beat seeds-in-pots for small scientists because the roots are visible through the glass. Label each jar with a face — happy bean, cupboard bean — and let your child draw the daily verdict; the drawing IS the observation record.

This lesson pairs with the What Plants Need flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Science, Nature & Discovery (Class 31).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SCIENCE, NATURE & DISCOVERY · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Seed — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson opens a package your child can hold: a seed is a baby plant with its lunch packed, waiting for two signals — warmth and water. Soak one, press it against clear glass, and the first root arrives where they can see it.

What is this?

A seed carries a tiny folded-up plant and a packed lunch of stored food, all inside one shell. When water soaks in and the weather warms, the shell splits, a root pushes down, a shoot pushes up, and the lunch feeds the journey until leaves take over.

What does it mean?

The seed is patient on purpose: sprouting into a cold snap would be the end, so it waits for warmth and damp — the go signal. Everything the sprout needs for its first days is already inside, which is why a seed can wake up in a jar with nothing but wet cotton.

What does the child need to know?

Soaking a seed overnight swells it and starts the wake-up. Some seeds ride the wind or hitch on animal fur before they land; others wait years underground for their moment. Beans are honest performers — big seeds, fast sprouting, visible roots.

Why this matters

Seeds make growth visible from day zero: your child plants it, marks the date, and witnesses the root before any leaf exists. The waiting is the skill — checking daily, drawing changes, learning that living things start small and unfold on their own schedule.

What it teaches

Patience and delayed observation (a real wait with daily checks), sequencing (root first, then shoot), early recording through date marks and drawings, and the wonder fact that a whole plant folds inside something palm-sized.

Words to learn

seedsproutrootshootsoilgrow

Say this to your child

“"Inside this little seed there is a baby plant, curled up tiny, with its first meals packed around it. Give it a long drink and some warmth, and it wakes: first a root to anchor and sip, then a shoot to find the sun. We do not make it grow — we just give it the go signal and watch."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: what is the child planting, and what is the green thing beside them? Name seed and sprout — before and after.
  2. Open the idea: a seed is a lunchbox with a baby plant folded inside, waiting for water and warmth to say go.
  3. Soak a bean overnight and compare: swollen versus dry. That puffing is the seed drinking its wake-up drink.
  4. Press the bean against the glass inside a clear jar, packed round with damp cotton, date-mark the jar, and guess what comes first — root or shoot?
  5. Check every day and draw what appears: root down, shoot up, then leaves. The lunch is eaten, the plant cooks for itself now.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: what is the child planting? Can you find the seed in the picture? What is growing beside the child — is it green? Is the soil dark or pale?

Ask your child

"What is hiding inside a seed?" "What tells a seed it is time to wake up?" "Which comes out first, a root or a shoot?" "Why did our bean get fat overnight?"

What your child can say or do

"The seed drank and got fat!" "The root came first — I was right!" Your child may soak everything in sight "to see if it wakes", plant a jar garden on every windowsill, or explain that a seed is "a lunchbox with a plant inside".

Out in the real world

Seeds are everywhere once you look: apple cores, sunflower packets, the dandelion clock your child blows, grass seeds under the mower. A packet of dried beans from the kitchen shelf is a full experiment kit — and sprouted beans can go straight into a pot of soil.

Try it together

Seed-sort kitchen botany: tip out a spoonful from the cupboard — beans, lentils, sunflower seeds, rice — and sort by size and colour, guessing which are seeds with plants inside. Then plant the biggest ones in a damp-cotton jar and race two kinds to a first root.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is inside a seed? What wakes it up? What grows first?" A baby plant and its lunch, water and warmth, the root = landed.

Parent tips

Clear jars pressed against the glass show the root weeks before any pot would — always plant one "for watching". Keep cotton damp, not swimming; mould is the jar garden’s only real enemy. If a seed fails, plant another: failures are data too.

This lesson pairs with the Seed flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Science, Nature & Discovery (Class 31).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SCIENCE, NATURE & DISCOVERY · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Tree Parts — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson upgrades the biggest plant your child knows from background scenery to a machine with named parts: roots that drink, a trunk that lifts, leaves that cook — all found on one walk, all touchable, one of them rub-able with crayons.

What is this?

A tree is built in three working parts: roots spread underground, drinking water and holding everything up; the trunk is the lift shaft hauling water to the crown; the leaves up top are the kitchen where sunshine turns into tree food.

What does it mean?

Every part has one job and the jobs chain together: drink, lift, cook. A tree is the plant-needs lesson standing up — water from below, light from above — scaled to a size your child can hug, and it lives in one place for decades doing the same three jobs.

What does the child need to know?

On a hot day a big tree hauls hundreds of buckets of water up its trunk. Roots peek above soil at the base — easy to find on old trees. Bark is the trunk’s armour, and every kind of tree wears its own pattern: rough oak, peeling birch, smooth beech.

Why this matters

Naming parts turns any tree into a readable system your child owns: here is the drinking bit, the lifting bit, the cooking bit. It scales the plant idea up, sets up bark-and-leaf collecting as a science hobby, and makes every street walk a tree tour.

What it teaches

System thinking with parts and jobs, tactile observation (bark rubbings, leaf textures), sorting and comparing collected leaves, and scale — the same plant plan, from bean jar to giant oak.

Words to learn

treerootstrunkbarkleavesbranches

Say this to your child

“"A tree is a three-part machine. The roots drink water from the soil, the trunk is the lift that carries the water up, up, up, and the leaves at the top catch sunshine and cook the tree’s food. Bark is the trunk’s armour — rub your crayon over it and it writes you its pattern."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: who is standing next to what, and is the tree taller than the child? Name the three parts — roots, trunk, leaves.
  2. Assign the jobs: roots drink underground, the trunk lifts the water all the way up, the leaves catch sunshine and cook.
  3. Find a big tree and inspect the base: can you see roots peeking out of the soil? That is the drinking crew, showing up for work.
  4. Rub the trunk: paper and a flat crayon over the bark print its armour pattern. Compare with the next tree — same pattern or different?
  5. Collect three fallen leaves — different shapes welcome — and finish the chain out loud: drink, lift, cook. The whole tree in three verbs.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: what is standing beside the child? Is the tree taller than the child? Can you find the trunk? Where are the leaves — up high or down low? What is the child looking at?

Ask your child

"Which part of the tree drinks?" "What does the trunk carry, and where to?" "What do the leaves do all summer?" "What is the bark for?"

What your child can say or do

"The trunk is a water lift!" "I can see the roots — they came out to wave!" Your child may hug every big tree on the walk, collect leaves by the carrier-bagful, or point out drinking roots and lifting trunks wherever trees grow.

Out in the real world

Trees are the fixed landmarks of childhood: the climbing tree, the conker tree, the one outside the window. Once parts have names, a walk becomes an inspection route — and a fallen big branch shows the rings inside, one ring per year, like a birthday count.

Try it together

Be the tree: your child crouches as roots (fingers wiggling underground), rises as the trunk (arms lifting, up, up), and bursts as leaves (hands fluttering at the top). Call the parts in any order; then swap and let them call your tree parts.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do roots do? What does the trunk do? What do leaves do?" Drink, lift, cook = landed.

Parent tips

Fallen leaves only — picking live leaves is stealing the tree’s kitchen, and your child can respect that. Bark rubbings work best on smooth bark with the paper taped down; label each rubbing with the tree’s spot so the collection becomes a map.

This lesson pairs with the Tree Parts flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Science, Nature & Discovery (Class 31).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SCIENCE, NATURE & DISCOVERY · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Cactus — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson takes the plant idea somewhere dry: if the rain almost never comes, how does anything stay alive? Your child meets the cactus as a survival engineer — a bottle-stem, needle-leaves, wax jacket — and squeezes a sponge to feel exactly why it works.

What is this?

A cactus is a plant built for the desert: its thick green stem swells up like a bottle and stores water for the dry weeks, its waxy skin seals moisture in, and its spines are actually leaves, shrunk to needles so they waste almost no water.

What does it mean?

Every plant needs water — the cactus just solved the problem differently. Where a garden plant drinks daily, the cactus drinks rarely and saves hard: wide stem to store, wax to seal, needles instead of thirsty flat leaves. Different home, different body, same needs.

What does the child need to know?

A full cactus can live on its stored water for months. Big desert cacti can weigh as much as a car or more — and most of that weight is water they saved. The spines double as armour: too sharp for thirsty animals to take a bite of the bottle.

Why this matters

The cactus stretches the plant-needs lesson into a new climate and plants the adaptation idea: living things fit their homes. It also answers the desert question — how? — with a body plan your child can model with two sponges in thirty seconds.

What it teaches

Cause-and-effect in a new habitat, adaptation thinking (bodies match homes), simple modelling with sponges, and careful-observation habits: where ARE the leaves on this plant, and why?

Words to learn

cactusdesertwaterstemspinesstore

Say this to your child

“"In the desert the rain forgets to come, so the cactus saves every drop it gets. Its fat stem swells up like a water bottle, its skin is sealed so the water cannot sneak out, and its leaves turned into needles — tiny, so they hardly drink at all. When rain finally falls, the bottle fills again."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: what is the child looking at, and what is the cactus growing in — grass or sand? Name the desert home.
  2. Ask the big question: it almost never rains there. How does anything drink? Collect guesses, then open the secret: the stem is a bottle.
  3. Find the leaves — trick question! They became the spines: needles so tiny they hardly lose any water, and too sharp for anyone to nibble.
  4. Run the sponge test: soak one sponge, leave one dry, squeeze both. Full sponge, full cactus — that is what a swollen stem means.
  5. Finish with the wax: cactus skin is sealed like a buttered jacket, holding the water in. Bottle, needles, wax jacket — three tricks, one survivor.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: what is the child looking at? Is the cactus tall or short? Can you find the spines? What is the cactus growing out of — grass, or dry sand?

Ask your child

"What does a cactus keep inside its fat stem?" "Why are the leaves needles instead of flat?" "How long can a cactus live on one big drink?" "Why does nothing try to eat the cactus?"

What your child can say or do

"The cactus is a water bottle plant!" "Its leaves turned into needles — that is so clever!" Your child may squeeze sponges at bath time explaining the desert, or point out cactus stems as bottles in every book, garden centre and cartoon.

Out in the real world

Desert thinking travels: camels store, seals thicken, your winter coat holds warm air — bodies solve their home’s biggest problem. House cacti bring it home literally: your child knows why the windowsill cactus gets one small drink and then is left alone for weeks.

Try it together

Sponge desert: soak two sponges, leave two dry, and line all four on a tray. Squeeze each in turn — which drip, which dust? Then build a cactus from a stuffed sock standing in a sand tray: fat bottle-stem, wax-paper jacket, and cocktail-stick spines only with a grown-up.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does a cactus store in its stem? What did its leaves become? Why the waxy skin?" Water, spines, to hold moisture in = landed.

Parent tips

The two-sponge squeeze is the whole lesson in the palm of a hand — do it twice. If a garden centre is nearby, walk the cactus shelf and let your child find the fattest bottle; watering rules can wait, the body plan is today’s win.

Staying safe

Cactus spines are real needles — house cacti stay up high where small hands cannot reach, and touching one is a grown-up job with tweezers on standby. The craft version follows the same rule: spines point up, fingers stay on the tray edge.

This lesson pairs with the Cactus flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Science, Nature & Discovery (Class 31).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SCIENCE, NATURE & DISCOVERY · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Mushroom — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson breaks the plant-animal pattern: a mushroom is the fruiting cap of a hidden fungus threading through damp soil and old wood. Your child learns where to predict them, what the hidden part does — and the one rule that is never up for negotiation.

What is this?

A mushroom is not a plant — it is one piece of a fungus, a living thing in its own category. Underground and inside old logs, thread-like fungus strands spread through damp places; when the time is right, a mushroom cap pops up to spread spores.

What does it mean?

Fungi are neither plant nor animal: they cannot cook their food with sunlight like plants, and they do not eat like animals — they soak up food from damp, decaying places. The mushroom you see is like the apple of a tree whose real body is hidden below.

What does the child need to know?

Mushrooms love damp: shady grass, rain-soft soil, old logs — after rain is mushroom o’clock. The cap opens like an umbrella to let spores drift off on the wind. Some wild kinds are poisonous, and that is why the family rule is look-only: shops and grown-ups pick what gets eaten.

Why this matters

Mushrooms open a third category in your child’s living-things map — plant, animal, fungus — which is a genuine scientific upgrade. The damp-rule also works as prediction: after rain, your child knows exactly where to look, and being right feels like magic.

What it teaches

Category thinking (a third kind of living thing), habitat prediction (damp spots after rain), respectful-distance discipline with wild things, and drawing or photographing as the way to collect what you must not touch.

Words to learn

mushroomfungusdampsporescapsoil

Say this to your child

“"A mushroom is not a plant and not an animal — it is a fungus. The real fungus lives underground as tiny threads, and the mushroom is just its fruit, pushing up when the ground is damp. We look with eyes and camera only — wild mushrooms are never food, because some kinds are poisonous."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: what is the child crouching beside, and what colour is the cap? Name it — a mushroom, and it is not a plant.
  2. Sort it out: plants cook with sunlight, animals eat, and fungi soak up food from damp, rotting places — a third kind of living thing.
  3. Tell the secret: the real fungus is threads under the ground; the mushroom is its apple, popped up to spread spores like tiny seeds.
  4. Predict together: where would a mushroom like to live — the dry sandpit or the shady corner under the tree? Then test after rain.
  5. Set the rule with its reason: wild mushrooms are never touched or tasted, because some kinds are poisonous, and it is always a grown-up or a shop that decides what gets eaten. We look, we photograph, we draw.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: what is the child crouching beside? What colour is the mushroom’s cap? Is it growing in the grass? How does the child look — curious, or careful?

Ask your child

"Is a mushroom a plant, an animal, or something else?" "Where do mushrooms like to grow?" "What is hiding under the ground?" "What is our rule about wild mushrooms — and why?"

What your child can say or do

"Mushrooms are fungus — a whole third thing!" "The mushroom is the fungus’s apple!" Your child may check the same damp corner after every rain, draw the caps they find instead of picking, or correct a grown-up who calls a mushroom a plant.

Out in the real world

Mushrooms shop-shelf versus garden-wild is the honest split: button mushrooms in the pack are food, wild caps are look-only. Yeast in bread and the fuzzy mould on forgotten fruit are the same category — fungus is hiding all over a normal week.

Try it together

Spore-print art: with a grown-up, place a shop-bought mushroom cap gills-down on dark paper under a cup overnight — next morning, a spore print! A soft round shadow the fungus made all by itself. Frame it: your child collected something without touching the wild.

Understanding check

Ask: "What three kinds of living things have we met? Where do mushrooms grow? Who decides what gets eaten?" Plant-animal-fungus, damp places, grown-ups = landed.

Parent tips

Wait for a rainy morning, then walk the same short loop — parks, hedge bases, old stumps — and let your child call the damp spots first. A photo collection titled "our mushrooms" beats any bouquet: it grows rain by rain, and nothing wilts.

Staying safe

Wild mushrooms are a never-eat, full stop: poisonous kinds can look almost exactly like safe ones, and no clever trick tells them apart — that decision belongs to grown-ups and shops alone. Touching a cap is safe; the habit to build is look, draw, photograph — because at four, hands-off has to hold even when no grown-up is watching.

This lesson pairs with the Mushroom flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Science, Nature & Discovery (Class 31).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SCIENCE, NATURE & DISCOVERY · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Pond Habitat — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson shrinks the whole idea of a habitat down to something a four-year-old can see edge to edge: a pond is one small home where frogs, snails, insects and water plants all fit together — and sitting still reveals more than any stomping.

What is this?

A pond is a small home shared by many living things: frogs hunt insects, snails graze the green slime on stones, water plants give shade and fresh air, and everyone finds food and shelter in the same little pool.

What does it mean?

Habitat means the place where an animal finds everything it needs — food, water, shelter — all in one spot. The pond works because the neighbours fit together: plants feed and shade, grazers clean, hunters hunt, and nobody has to leave home to survive.

What does the child need to know?

Pond residents come in layers: swimmers below, floaters on the surface, jumpers at the edge, divers at the bottom. Even the water itself is crowded with tiny life. The stillness rule is real biology — loud stomping sends frogs diving; sitting quietly brings the pond back out.

Why this matters

A pond is a whole ecosystem at child scale — small enough to see across, busy enough to show sharing. It gathers the set’s animals into one home and teaches the biggest ecology idea gently: animals belong where their needs are met.

What it teaches

Sustained quiet watching (four still minutes is a real achievement), counting and tallying, the habitat idea of needs-met-in-one-place, and respect for shared homes: visitors do not fish, grab or empty the pond.

Words to learn

pondhabitathomefrogsnailplants

Say this to your child

“"A pond is one small home with a lot of tenants. The plants make shade and fresh air, the snails scrub the stones, the insects feed the frogs, and everyone finds dinner without ever leaving home. We sit still like visitors — and the pond forgets we are here and starts its show."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: what is the child leaning over, and who is sitting on the lily pad? Name the pond as a home, not just water.
  2. List the tenants: frogs, snails, insects, fish, water plants — everyone shares this one small pool.
  3. Explain the fit: the plants make shade and fresh air, the snails graze the stones clean, the frogs hunt the insects. Neighbours with jobs.
  4. Run the pond-sit: four still minutes, arm’s length from the edge, tallying every living thing you spot — swimmers, floaters, jumpers, gliders.
  5. Compare tallies: stillness finds more than stomping ever will. Ask which neighbours your child would want in their own home — and why the frog never leaves.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: what is the child leaning over? Can you find the frog? What is the frog sitting on? Who else do you think lives in this water?

Ask your child

"Who shares the pond as their home?" "What do the water plants give the pond?" "Why do we sit still at a pond?" "What does a habitat give the animals that live there?"

What your child can say or do

"The pond is everyone’s house!" "I counted five things alive — a frog, a snail, and three tiny swimmers!" Your child may play ponds in the paddling pool, assign every toy a pond job, or shush the family at the water’s edge: "quiet — the frogs are coming out."

Out in the real world

Habitat logic applies everywhere once your child sees it in miniature: a log is a beetle’s pond, a hedge is a wren’s, your garden is one big shared home. The pond version is just the clearest — small, visible edges, tenants on display all summer.

Try it together
