Pond in a bowl pretend: blue cloth for water, corks for floating snails, a toy frog on a paper lily pad, cut-out plants for shade. Your child stocks the habitat, then plays the pond-sit: who comes out when the room goes quiet? Add visitors one by one — who eats whom?

Understanding check

Ask: "What is a habitat? Who shares a pond? What does stillness find?" A home with everything needed, frogs snails insects plants, more = landed.

Parent tips

Pick a pond with a bench or a flat bank and go at mid-morning, when frogs bask and pond skaters skate. If no pond is near, a wildlife documentary pond scene or a garden water-butt with wrigglers works — the stillness habit is the portable part.

Staying safe

Pond edges are the one hard rule: water deeper than a puddle means a grown-up holds a small hand the whole time — slippery banks and deep mud tip little feet faster than anyone expects. The pond-sit happens sitting down, at a distance from the edge, and nothing goes into the water — not hands, not nets, not toes.

This lesson pairs with the Pond Habitat flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Science, Nature & Discovery (Class 31).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SCIENCE, NATURE & DISCOVERY · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Cloud — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson lifts the weather into reach: clouds are crowds of tiny water drops floating high, and your child can make one on a cold window with a single breath — then read the sky, white for shape-finding, grey for rain incoming.

What is this?

A cloud is made of tiny drops of water floating in the air — so small that the air holds them up. When many drops crowd together, the cloud turns grey and heavy, and the drops join until they are big enough to fall as rain.

What does it mean?

Clouds are the sky’s visible water: the sun lifts moisture up as vapour, invisible, and crowds of drops are what it looks like when that vapour gathers high up. White means widely spread and light; grey means packed and ready to pour.

What does the child need to know?

A small-looking cloud can weigh as much as a herd of elephants — the drops are just spread across a huge space. Fog is a cloud that has come down to the ground, and you can walk through it. Cloud shapes shift constantly: the crowd is always moving.

Why this matters

Clouds answer "where does rain come from?" before it rains, and the breath-on-the-window trick makes the material touchable: your own breath carries water, and it turns to visible drops on cold glass — a cloud in miniature, made by your child.

What it teaches

Sky-watching as a daily habit, shape-finding imagination on moving clouds, cause-and-effect (crowded drops, grey, rain), and the breath experiment’s lesson that invisible water is real and everywhere — including inside us.

Words to learn

clouddropsfloatgreyskyfog

Say this to your child

“"A cloud is a crowd of tiny water drops floating high in the sky. Each drop is so small the air holds it up, but when the drops crowd close together the cloud turns grey and heavy — and then the drops tumble down as rain. Breathe on the window: you just made a baby cloud."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: what is the child pointing at? Is the cloud big or small? Name it — a floating crowd of tiny water drops.
  2. Ask the stumper: clouds are heavy with water — why do they not fall? Because the drops are tiny and the air holds them up high.
  3. Make a mini-cloud: breathe on a cold window or mirror and watch the mist appear — your breath carried water, and the cold glass gathered it into drops.
  4. Read the sky together: white puffy clouds for shape-finding — a bunny, a boat — and grey-packed clouds for rain coming. Which is overhead today?
  5. Drop the fog fact: fog is a cloud that came down to visit. You can walk through a cloud — you probably already have.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: what is the child pointing at? Is the cloud big in the sky? What shape does the cloud look like to you? Can you find more clouds — or is the sky nearly clear?

Ask your child

"What are clouds made of?" "Why do clouds float instead of falling?" "What does it mean when a cloud turns grey?" "What did your breath make on the window?"

What your child can say or do

"Clouds are made of tiny drops — elephants’ worth!" "I made a cloud on the window with my breath!" Your child may read the sky out loud every morning — "grey today, rain incoming" — or blow on cold windows on purpose to grow mist.

Out in the real world

Clouds are the daily forecast your child can read: the white-building day for kite flying, the flat grey blanket for wellies, the fog walk to nursery where the world goes soft. Shape games on a picnic blanket, grey-watching before a walk — the sky is the toy.

Try it together

Cotton-wool sky: glue cotton balls onto blue paper — stretched thin for wispy clouds, bunched high for towering ones, pressed flat and grey-tinted for rain clouds. Then lie back on the rug and find shapes in each other’s cotton clouds before checking the real sky.

Understanding check

Ask: "What are clouds made of? Why do they float? What does grey mean?" Tiny water drops, the air holds them, rain is coming = landed.

Parent tips

Morning is best for cloud watching — shape-hunting works before the day fills up. The window-breath trick needs genuinely cold glass; on warm days, a fridge-chilled mirror does it. Grey-sky days get a bonus: fog is the walk-through cloud your child can finally touch.

This lesson pairs with the Cloud flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Science, Nature & Discovery (Class 31).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SCIENCE, NATURE & DISCOVERY · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Rain — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson turns a rainy day into the point: rain is the sky returning the water the sun lifted up, and your child can watch the whole trip from the window — then map the puddles it leaves behind and learn that this water has been round this loop forever.

What is this?

Rain happens because sunshine lifts water up — out of seas, puddles and plants — as vapour too small to see. High above, the vapour gathers into clouds; when the drops inside grow heavy, they fall as rain, watering everything below before the trip starts over.

What does it mean?

Rain is not the sky leaking — it is one step of a loop: up as vapour, along in clouds, down as drops, away in rivers and puddles, and back up again. The water falling today is the same water that has been going round this planet since long before us.

What does the child need to know?

Vapour is water you cannot see — it is floating past right now. A rainy-day drop once splashed on dinosaurs: the loop is that old. Rain lands as drips, drops or downpours, and every puddle is the sky’s delivery, waiting for the sun to lift it back.

Why this matters

The water cycle answers the question every child asks — where does rain come from? — honestly and simply, and it makes rainy days purposeful: the garden is being watered, the puddles are a map, and the window is the weather station.

What it teaches

Understanding a circular story (a loop with no beginning or end), weather vocabulary and reporting, observation from a fixed post (the window), and the deep-time wow: same water, dinosaurs, today.

Words to learn

rainclouddropsvapourpuddleheavy

Say this to your child

“"Sunshine lifts water up out of the sea and the puddles — as vapour, so small you cannot see it. Up high it gathers into clouds, and when the drops get heavy the sky lets them go: rain! Puddles form, the sun lifts them up again, and the whole trip starts over. That water has been going round for ages."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: what is the child wearing, and where is the rain coming from? Find the cloud — the rain’s delivery van.
  2. Tell the loop: sunshine turns water into invisible vapour that floats up, clouds gather it, and when the drops inside get heavy, down it comes. Up, along, down, around.
  3. Report from the window: how heavy is the rain — drips, drops, or pouring? Say it like a weather reporter on TV.
  4. Map the puddles after: which is biggest, which dries first, and where did the water go when the sun came back? Up — again.
  5. Land the deep fact: this exact water has been round the loop for millions of years — the rain outside once splashed on dinosaurs.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: what is the child wearing — a raincoat, or a sun hat? Where is the rain falling from? Can you find the cloud? Is the child watching the rain or running away from it?

Ask your child

"Where does rain come from?" "What is vapour?" "What happens to a puddle when the sun comes out?" "How heavy is the rain today — drips, drops or pouring?"

What your child can say or do

"The rain is the water coming back down!" "My puddle got lifted up — I saw it dry!" Your child may deliver window weather reports every wet morning, jump puddles while announcing "the clouds got heavy", or comfort a grey day: "the garden is getting its drink."

Out in the real world

The loop is visible all week: kettle steam, damp pavement drying after rain, fog on the bathroom mirror — water, changing place and form. Once your child owns the loop, rain stops being a cancelled plan and becomes the most interesting thing the sky does.

Try it together

Water-cycle in a bag: with a grown-up, tape a zip bag with a splash of water high on a sunny window. Mark the water line. Over days, drops climb the bag wall — evaporated up, gathered at the top, and raining back down when heavy enough. The whole loop, hanging in the sun.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where does rain come from? What lifts the water up? What happens to puddles in the sun?" Clouds, the sun, they dry back up = landed.

Parent tips

Keep the window post safe and warm — rain watching is an inside sport, with wellies saved for the puddle map afterwards. If thunder joins the rain, come inside and leave the counting to the grown-ups — the loop story keeps for the next dry day.

This lesson pairs with the Rain flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Science, Nature & Discovery (Class 31).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SCIENCE, NATURE & DISCOVERY · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Rain Helps Plants — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson flips the rainy-day grump: while everyone runs inside, the whole garden sits down to drink. Your child learns that rain is a watering can for every plant outside — and takes an after-rain tour to see exactly who has been drinking.

What is this?

Plants are always drinking — their roots sip water from the soil non-stop — and rain refills the soil faster than any hose. Drops land on leaves, trickle down stems, and sink into the dark earth where the roots are waiting to slurp it all up.

What does it mean?

Rain is weather on the plant’s side: a whole night of rain does more for the garden than an afternoon of watering, because it soaks deep where roots actually reach. The garden is not getting wet — it is getting fed, and the soil is the cup it drinks from.

What does the child need to know?

Roots do the drinking, not the leaves — raindrops on a leaf are just passing through on their way down. After rain the soil turns dark and damp, leaves wear beads of water, and worms come up for the wet. A dry week makes plants droop; rain perks them back up.

Why this matters

This card connects weather to growth: rain is not a nuisance, it is lunch for every plant outside. It gives your child a reason to be glad about wet days, links the plant-needs lesson to the sky, and makes the watering chore feel like helping the rain.

What it teaches

Linking weather to plant growth (cause and effect across a whole garden), after-rain observation of soil, leaves and worms, empathy with living things (the garden was thirsty), and patience — the tour works best a day after the rain.

Words to learn

rainplantsrootsdrinksoilgarden

Say this to your child

“"When it rains, the whole garden sits down to eat — or really, to drink. The drops run off the leaves, down the stems, into the soil, and the roots slurp it up like straws. A whole night of rain is the best meal the garden ever gets. That is why rainy days are actually garden days."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: what is the seedling getting, and what is the child wearing? Name it — the garden’s watering day.
  2. Ask the flip question: what happens to the plants outside when it rains all day? The garden is not hiding from rain — it is drinking it.
  3. Explain the straws: roots sip constantly from the soil, and rain refills the soil cup deep down where straws reach. Drops on leaves just trickle home.
  4. Take the after-rain tour: find leaves wearing raindrop beads, press a finger into dark damp soil, and count the worms that came up for the wet.
  5. Connect to home: your watering can does for pots what the sky does for gardens — and after a rainy week, the pots get a day off.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: what is falling on the seedling? What is the child wearing in the picture? Is the seedling big or small? What do you think the seedling will grow into after its drink?

Ask your child

"Which part of a plant drinks the rain?" "Where do the raindrops on a leaf go next?" "What does the soil look like after rain?" "Why are rainy days good for the garden?"

What your child can say or do

"Rainy days are garden drinking days!" "The worms came up because they like the wet!" Your child may refuse to grumble on wet days now, check the soil with one finger after rain, or explain to a worried plant-waterer that the sky has the shift covered.

Out in the real world

Rain’s work shows all around: drooping tomatoes perk up overnight, the lawn greens by the weekend, rain-fed gardens outgrow watered pots. After the next dry spell your child can run the reverse check — which plants missed the sky’s watering can?

Try it together

Watering-can relay: paper plants around the room, one cup of "rain" per runner — sprinkle each plant gently at the base, not the leaves, because roots do the drinking. Then a slow-motion after-rain tour of your own: leaves, soil, and one lucky worm hunt outside.

Understanding check

Ask: "Who drinks the rain — leaves or roots? Where does the water collect? What is a rainy day for the garden?" Roots, the soil, a big drink = landed.

Parent tips

Do the finger-test of damp soil together after every rain — one gentle poke, two centimetres down — and your child will soon read the garden’s thirst by touch. Welly weather is tour weather: the wetter the walk, the more the garden shows.

This lesson pairs with the Rain Helps Plants flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Science, Nature & Discovery (Class 31).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SCIENCE, NATURE & DISCOVERY · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Rainbow — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson cracks the sky’s best trick: white sunlight is secretly a whole family of colors, and raindrops are the mirrors that split it apart. Your child learns the two-ingredient recipe — sun behind, drops in front — then makes a rainbow on demand with a spray.

What is this?

A rainbow appears when sunlight shines through falling raindrops: each drop splits the white light into its colors, and millions of drops together paint an arc across the sky. Sun AND rain, each in its place, or no rainbow at all.

What does it mean?

White light is a mix hiding in plain sight — a raindrop is a tiny prism that unmixes it. The recipe needs both ingredients at once: sun on one side, drops on the other. That is why rainbows visit while rain is leaving, not while it is pouring on your head.

What does the child need to know?

Look carefully and a rainbow carries seven colors: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet. The rule for finding one: stand with the sun behind you and the drops in front. The same trick works with a hose mist or a spray bottle on any sunny day.

Why this matters

Rainbows are light science your child can point at and even manufacture — the spray-bottle recipe turns waiting for weather into making it. The two-conditions rule (sun behind, drops ahead) is also early cause-and-effect: no ingredients, no rainbow.

What it teaches

Observation of a fleeting phenomenon, counting and naming colors in order, cause-and-effect with two required ingredients, and the maker-mindset: recreating nature’s trick at garden-hose scale.

Words to learn

rainbowlightcolorsraindropssunarc

Say this to your child

“"Sunlight looks white, but inside it hides every color you can name. When sun shines through raindrops, each little drop splits the light like a prism — and a whole arc of drops paints the rainbow across the sky. Want the recipe? Sun behind you, rain in front. We can even make one with the spray bottle!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: what is the child looking up at, and can you name the colors you see? Count them together, top to bottom.
  2. Tell the secret: sunlight looks white, but it is secretly carrying every color — a raindrop splits it apart like a key opening a box of paints.
  3. Learn the recipe: sun behind you, drops in front of you — both at once, or nothing appears. That is why rainbows come out as rain moves away.
  4. Make your own: on a sunny day, stand with your back to the sun and spray a fine mist into the air — a small rainbow hangs in the water.
  5. Play color spotter: find all seven in the arc, then hunt them off the sky — red postbox, yellow banana, violet plum. The rainbow’s family is everywhere.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: what is the child looking up at? How many colors can you find in the rainbow? Can you name one of them? Does the child look happy to see it?

Ask your child

"What two things do you need to make a rainbow?" "Where does the sun need to be standing?" "What does a raindrop do to white light?" "How many colors live in a rainbow?"

What your child can say or do

"Sunlight has all the colors hiding inside!" "Sun behind, drops in front — I can make one!" Your child may carry the spray bottle on every sunny walk, demand rainbow checks during every shower, or name the seven colors in order like a spell.

Out in the real world

Rainbow conditions show up weekly: sun shower, spray at the fountains, the hose on the lawn. Once your child knows the recipe, they stop waiting and start engineering — back to the sun, mist in the air, and there it hangs. Bubbles and CDs carry the same color-splitting trick indoors.

Try it together

Prism stations: a glass of water on a sunny windowsill throws a small rainbow on the floor; a CD under a lamp scatters colors; bubbles wear moving ones. Send your child on a rainbow hunt around the house — where else does light get split apart?

Understanding check

Ask: "What two things make a rainbow? Where does the sun stand? What does a drop do to light?" Sun and raindrops, behind you, splits it into colors = landed.

Parent tips

The spray-bottle rainbow takes a try or two — fine mist, low sun, and your back squarely to it. Morning and evening sun make the biggest arcs. If the real sky delivers one, drop everything and run out: a first wild rainbow is a core memory.

This lesson pairs with the Rainbow flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Science, Nature & Discovery (Class 31).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SCIENCE, NATURE & DISCOVERY · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Wind — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson cracks the hardest idea a preschooler meets — invisible things are real — with the friendliest possible evidence: the wind. Your child cannot see air, but they can see everything it pushes, feel it on their face, and hold a streamer up to catch it working.

What is this?

Wind is air on the move. Air itself stays invisible, but everything it pushes gives it away: kites lifting, leaves tumbling, flags snapping, hair flying, washing swinging. A gentle breeze is a small push; a gust is a big one.

What does it mean?

You cannot see the wind, but you can see what it does — that is evidence, the scientist’s way of knowing something without eyes on it. Still air is real too: it is what your child is breathing right now, and it only shows itself when it moves.

What does the child need to know?

Moving air does real work: it pushes boats with sails, spins windmills, dries the washing and lifts kites high. A paper streamer hangs limp in still air and streams flat when the wind blows — a wind meter made from one strip of paper.

Why this matters

Wind teaches proof-by-effect: how do you know something invisible is there? Watch what it moves. That habit — evidence over eyesight — transfers to sound, gravity and germs later, and it makes every windy walk a science field.

What it teaches

Evidence-based reasoning (seeing effects, not the thing), weather awareness, cause-and-effect at speed (gusts come and go), and physical play — leaning into wind, catching leaves, feeling pushes on cheeks and chest.

Words to learn

windairpushbreezekiteleaves

Say this to your child

“"Nobody has ever seen the wind — but we can see everything it pushes! Kites lift, leaves tumble, flags flap, your hair goes everywhere. When you feel a push on your face, that is air moving past. Even still air is real: you are breathing it in and out right now."”

Step by step

  1. Look at the card: what is the child holding, and what is lifting the kite? Trick question — can you SEE the wind itself?
  2. Set the detective case: the wind is invisible, so how do we know it is there? Because we can see everything it pushes.
  3. Play the moving hunt: outdoors, tally five things the wind is pushing — leaves, flags, hair, washing, clouds. Count them out loud.
  4. Make the meter: a paper streamer on a stick — hanging means still air, streaming means the wind is working. Test it high and low.
  5. Feel the proof: stand into the breeze, cheeks out. The push you feel is air, and air is real even when it stands still — you are breathing some right now.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: what is in the child’s hands? Is the kite going up or coming down? What do you think is lifting the kite? Can you see the wind itself anywhere in the picture?

Ask your child

"What is the wind made of?" "How do we know the wind is there if we cannot see it?" "What did your streamer do in still air?" "What can strong wind push — a leaf or a boat?"

What your child can say or do

"I cannot see the wind but I can see it PUSHING!" "Still air hangs my streamer down." Your child may appoint themselves official wind reporter on every walk, hold paper streamers out on the balcony, or explain that wind is "air on the run".

Out in the real world

Wind signs are everywhere once you are the detective: drying washing, rustling hedges, dust drifting down the street, clouds racing overhead. Windmills and sailboats are the big-league versions — moving air doing heavy work, exactly like your child’s kite.

Try it together

Wind duel: hold a feather race — who can blow their feather across the table using only breath-wind? Then fan-test: paper plate fans, curtain waves, a huffing-puffing relay. Finish outside on the next gusty day with a homemade streamer on a stick.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is wind? How do we know it is there? What did the streamer show?" Moving air, the pushes we can see, still or streaming = landed.

Parent tips

The streamer meter is the keep-forever tool — tape one to the garden fence or balcony rail and your child reads the wind over breakfast. Gusty days are kite days; still days are feather-breath days. Both are the same lesson at two speeds.

This lesson pairs with the Wind flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Science, Nature & Discovery (Class 31).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SCIENCE, NATURE & DISCOVERY · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Ice — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson makes states of matter touchable — literally: one substance, two shapes, back and forth on demand. Your child freezes water, melts it again, and runs the melt race that shows cold making solid and warmth setting it free.

What is this?

Ice is water that got so cold it froze into a solid — the same water, wearing a hard shape. Add warmth and the ice gives up, melts, and turns back into liquid water. Cold freezes, warmth melts; back and forth as many times as you like.

What does it mean?

One substance, two costumes: water is a liquid that pours, ice is the same water standing still. Nothing is lost in the change — a vanished ice cube is a puddle in disguise, which is why melting is not disappearing, just changing back.

What does the child need to know?

Water is the everyday thing that shows up in all three forms: solid ice, liquid water, and invisible vapour in the air. Ice floats in your drink because frozen water puffs up slightly bigger than it was. Freezers make ice by stealing heat; warm hands give it back.

Why this matters

Ice is the friendliest states-of-matter lesson there is: your kitchen can run it daily, the change is visible, fast and reversible. It builds cold-warm causality — temperature as a cause with visible effects — and the conservation idea that stuff does not vanish.

What it teaches

Cause-and-effect with temperature, reversible-change thinking (freeze and melt, freeze again), prediction and fair testing in the melt race, and vocabulary — solid, melt, freeze — that will carry through every later science lesson.

Words to learn

icewaterfreezemeltcoldwarm

Say this to your child

“"Ice is just water that got very, very cold — the same water, frozen into a hard little shape. Hold it in your warm hand and the warmth melts it back into water: it did not disappear, it changed its costume! Cold freezes, warmth melts, and you can run the trick all day."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: what is the child holding? Does it look cold or warm? Name it — water’s hard, frozen costume.
  2. Run the freeze: fill a tray with water, pop it in the freezer, and check an hour later. Same water — where did the wobble go?
  3. Explain the trade: cold freezes water solid, warmth melts it back. Nothing disappears — a "vanished" cube is a puddle in disguise.
  4. Race the melt: one cube on a warm palm, one on a cool plate — which gives up first? Why? Warmth is the melt-maker, so the palm wins.
  5. Find the puddle under the loser and ask where the ice went: it changed back. Freeze it again tonight — the show repeats forever.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: what is the child holding? Does the ice cube look big or small? What do you think the ice feels like — bumpy, smooth, slippery? Where do you think the child got it?

Ask your child

"What is ice made of?" "What melts ice back into water?" "Where did the ice cube go when it vanished?" "What does the freezer do to water?"

What your child can say or do

"The ice didn’t vanish — it melted back into water!" "My hand is a melt-machine!" Your child may run melt races on every warm surface, rescue cubes from the freezer to "free" them, or explain that winter puddles are "just water wearing its cold costume".

Out in the real world

Ice works everywhere: drinks clinking in summer, frost on the grass in winter, the freezer’s cold boxes on picnics. Melting is daily too — ice lollies drip, frost fades off the car windscreen, and snowman puddles tell the same story every January.

Try it together

Ice treasure rescue: freeze small toys into a tub of water, then hand your child a cup of warm water and a spoon to excavate them. Warmth melts, tools chip, treasures pop free. Afterwards, leave one chunk on the plate and watch it confess: it was water all along.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is ice? What does warmth do to it? Where does a melted cube go?" Frozen water, melts it, back to being water = landed.

Parent tips

Freeze treasure tubs the night before — the rescue buys twenty focused minutes, and the warm-water spoon teaches control. Keep the melt race fair: same-size cubes, started at the same moment. Your palm wins, but the cool plate teaches the patience half of warmth.

This lesson pairs with the Ice flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Science, Nature & Discovery (Class 31).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SCIENCE, NATURE & DISCOVERY · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Rock — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the cheapest science hobby on Earth: rock collecting. Your child gathers five stones, breaks the all-rocks-are-grey assumption, and sorts a pocketful by feel, weight and shine — classification practice with a museum that fits in a shoebox.

What is this?

Rocks are hard pieces of Earth itself — the ground is made of them. Some rocks cooled from hot melted rock, some were pressed in layers over ages, and pebbles are rocks that water and weather rolled smooth. Inside many rocks, sparkling specks called minerals hide.

What does it mean?

Rocks are not all alike — they differ in color, texture, weight and shine, and sorting those differences is real science. Every pebble is a story: a sharp rock sanded round by years of waves, rain and rolling until it fits perfectly in a small palm.

What does the child need to know?

Rocks come from different recipes: cooled lava, pressed mud layers, and minerals that sparkle when the light catches them. A smooth beach pebble took ages to tumble round. Geologists — rock scientists — read those clues to tell Earth’s story.

Why this matters

Rock sorting is classification practice with instant feedback: bumpy or smooth, heavy or light, grey or sparkly — and no two collections match. It also grounds your child literally: the ground under everything has names, histories and surprises.

What it teaches

Classification by properties (color, texture, weight, shine), close looking with a magnifier, collecting and caring for a set, and the long-time idea — smoothness that takes years, layers that take longer.

Words to learn

rockpebblesmoothhardmineralsort

Say this to your child

“"Rocks are pieces of the Earth itself — the whole ground is made of them. Some came from hot melted rock gone hard, some were pressed in layers, and every smooth pebble was rolled round by water over years and years. Look inside: those sparkling specks are minerals, the ingredients rocks are cooked from."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: what is the child examining, and what are they looking through? Is the rock smooth or bumpy? Name the tool — a magnifying glass.
  2. Break the assumption: are all rocks grey? Hunt for pink, white, speckled, striped — rocks are Earth’s mixed recipe box.
  3. Collect five: parks, paths, beaches — five different stones, each one chosen for a reason. Why THIS one?
  4. Sort your own way: by color, by feel, by weight, by shine — then re-sort by a new rule. Scientists sort and re-sort all the time.
  5. Look close: specks that sparkle are minerals, the ingredients inside. And the smoothest pebble? Water rolled it round for years before your child found it.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: what is the child examining? What are they looking through? Is the rock smooth or bumpy? What color is the rock — grey, or something else?

Ask your child

"What is a rock a piece of?" "How did the smooth pebble get so smooth?" "What are the sparkling specks inside rocks called?" "How many ways can you sort your five rocks?"

What your child can say or do

"Minerals are the sparkles inside!" "My pebble got smooth from the waves rolling it!" Your child may start a shoebox museum with labelled favourites, sort every gravel patch on the walk, or hand you the heaviest rock and ask you to guess its weight.

Out in the real world

Rocks are the floor of childhood: driveways, riverbanks, the beach, the gravel by the school gate. The collection grows every trip, and the sorting never ends — by weight, by shine, by which one looks most like a potato. Museums upgrade it later; the habit starts now.

Try it together

Pebble-washing day: rinse and brush the collection in a basin, lay it out on a towel, and sort into trays — sparkles, stripes, smoothest, heaviest. Then a tumbler demo: a jar, a splash of sand and one sugar cube, shaken gently, shows edges wearing round like the sea does it.

Understanding check

Ask: "What are rocks pieces of? What made the pebble smooth? What are the sparkles called?" Earth, water rolling it, minerals = landed.

Parent tips

Set a pick-up limit before the walk — five is plenty — and a display box after. A cheap magnifying glass doubles the pleasure: sparkles, stripes and sand-grains are all hiding in plain pebbles. Say yes to the pocketful; the collecting instinct is the science.

This lesson pairs with the Rock flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Science, Nature & Discovery (Class 31).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SCIENCE, NATURE & DISCOVERY · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Sun — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson names the engine behind nearly everything your child has learned: plants, weather, shadows, day and night — all run on the sun. One star, 150 million kilometres away, delivers light and warmth straight to the palm of a hand.

What is this?

The sun is a star — a giant ball of burning-bright gas — and the closest one to Earth. It pours out light and warmth in every direction; a small share lands on us, and that share makes our daytime, grows our food and warms our skin.

What does it mean?

Every other star is a much farther sun: pinpricks of light at night are the same kind of giant ball, just too far to feel. The sun is the engine behind the garden — plants cook with its light, puddles dry from its warmth, and shadows point away from it.

What does the child need to know?

The sun’s warmth travels about 150 million kilometres to reach your hand — and you can feel it. Light and warmth are gifts, but staring is not: looking straight at the sun damages eyes, and sunglasses do not make staring safe. Shade, hats and looking away are the rule.

Why this matters

The sun ties the whole science set together — plants, weather, shadows, the moon’s shine, day and night all borrow its power. Naming it as a star upgrades the night sky: your child now knows that stars are suns, and one of them is ours.

What it teaches

Connecting earlier lessons to one power source (plants, weather, shadows), scale thinking (a star we can feel versus stars we only see), sensory evidence for warmth, and safety rules with reasons that stick.

Words to learn

sunstarlightwarmthshadowshade

Say this to your child

“"The sun is our star — the closest one, a huge ball of burning light and warmth. Its light makes our day, its warmth grows the plants, and you can feel it right on your hand. But it is too bright for eyes: staring is off the table, sunglasses or not. We enjoy the sun by feeling it and looking away."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: what is the child doing with their hands, and why? Shading the eyes — exactly what smart sun-watchers do.
  2. Name it: the sun is a star, the closest one — every other star in the night sky is a far-off sun of its own.
  3. Feel the delivery: press one palm flat on a sun-baked wall, one on a shaded wall. Feel that difference? The warmth crossed 150 million kilometres to get here.
  4. Trace the power: plants cook with sun light, puddles dry in sun warmth, shadows point away from the sun. One star, half the set’s lessons.
  5. Set the rule with its reason: the sun is too bright to look at — staring can damage young eyes for good, and sunglasses do not make staring safe. We feel the sun; we never stare.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: what is the child doing with their hands? Is the sun smiling in the picture? Is the child smiling too? Why do you think the child is shading their eyes instead of looking right at it?

Ask your child

"What is the sun — a planet or a star?" "What does the sun give us?" "How far did the warmth on your hand travel?" "Why do we never stare at the sun?"

What your child can say or do

"The sun is a star — OUR star!" "Every star is a sun, just far, far away!" Your child may feel walls, pavements and railings for sun warmth and report the heat, shade their eyes like a salute on every sunny walk, or correct anyone who calls the sun a planet.

Out in the real world

Sun power is daily life: washing drying, tomatoes ripening, the hot slide at noon, the cold side of the house in shade. Once your child names the sun as the engine, the garden becomes a powered system — and the night sky becomes a field of far-off suns to wonder at.

Try it together

Warmth treasure hunt: find five warm things the sun made — a sunny wall, a metal railing, the car bonnet, a paving stone, the sandbox — and five cool things in shade. Rank them hottest to coolest. The sun’s fingerprints, collected by hand.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is the sun? What does it give us? Can we look straight at it?" Our nearest star, light and warmth, never — and now we know why = landed.

Parent tips

Run the two-wall warmth compare on every sunny day — the palm test never gets old. Midday summer sun is hat, shade and water-bottle weather; the science lesson pairs perfectly with the practical one. Save star-gazing for after dark: the night sky is the sun’s family photo.

Staying safe

The sun is a never-stare rule, full stop: looking straight at it burns the light-catching back of the eye, and the damage is permanent — sunglasses are for comfort, not permission. Shade and hats do the protecting on bright days, and the warm-wall test is the safe way to study the sun: feel it, never face it.

This lesson pairs with the Sun flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Science, Nature & Discovery (Class 31).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SCIENCE, NATURE & DISCOVERY · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Moon — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson hands your child the sky object they can actually watch change: the moon. No telescope needed — a window, a diary and a month of checking reveals borrowed light, changing shapes, and the day-shift moon that sometimes shows up before bed.

What is this?

The moon is a rocky ball circling Earth, and it glows only with borrowed light — sunlight lands on it and bounces back, like a torch on a mirror. As the month goes round, we see the lit part from different angles: crescent, half, full.

What does it mean?

Moonlight is second-hand sunlight: the moon is a reflector, not a lamp. The changing shape is not the moon being nibbled — it is the same rocky ball, lit from one side, while we watch from a moving Earth. The shapes are geometry your child can see for free.

What does the child need to know?

The moon has no wind and no rain, so astronauts’ footprints from decades ago are still pressed in its dust, fresh as the day they landed. Some nights the moon hides; some mornings it takes the early shift, hanging pale in the daytime sky.

Why this matters

The moon is the nightly observation habit your child can own — no equipment, one drawing a day. Learning that its shine is borrowed links the moon back to the sun, and the changing shapes teach that watching over time is how you see slow things happen.

What it teaches

Long-horizon observation (a month-long diary), recording with drawings, the reflection idea (shining by borrowed light), and comfort with the moon’s pattern — the same shapes return, which is what makes them predictable.

Words to learn

moonnightlightcrescentfullsky

Say this to your child

“"The moon does not glow by itself — it is a big rocky ball, and the sun lights it up like a torch shining on a mirror. That is why its shape seems to change: we see the sunny side from different angles all month. And get this — the footprints astronauts left there are still there, because the moon has no wind to blow them away."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: what is the child looking through, and what are they looking at? Name it — Earth’s rocky companion.
  2. Ask the trick question: does the moon make its own light? No — the sun shines on it and the moon bounces the light back, like a mirror.
  3. Start the moon diary: draw its shape tonight — crescent, half, or full? Date every drawing. Some nights it hides; those count too.
  4. Check the early shift: look for the moon before bed AND in the morning — sometimes it hangs pale in the daytime sky.
  5. Explain the shapes: nothing is eating the moon — it is one ball, lit from one side, and we see the lit part from different angles as the month goes round.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: what is the child looking through? What can they see in the sky? Is the picture set at night or in the day? What shape is the moon in the picture?

Ask your child

"Does the moon make its own light?" "Where does the moon’s light come from?" "Why does the moon seem to change shape?" "Why are the astronauts’ footprints still there?"

What your child can say or do

"The moon is a mirror for the sun!" "No wind, no rain — the footprints stay forever!" Your child may guard their moon diary like a treasure, report the moon’s shape from the car window, or shout "day-shift moon!" when it shows up over breakfast.

Out in the real world

The moon is nightly, free and impossible to miss once your child is looking: dog-walk crescents, bath-time full moons, the pale daytime moon over the school run. The diary turns "always there" into "always changing on a schedule" — a pattern your child can crack in one month.

Try it together

Ball-and-torch moon: in a dim room, shine a torch (the sun) on a ball (the moon) and let your child walk around it, watching the lit shape change from crescent to full as the angle changes. Then draw tonight’s real moon and compare it to the model.

Understanding check

Ask: "Does the moon make its own light? Why does its shape change? What makes the moon shine?" No — borrowed, angles, sunlight bouncing back = landed.

Parent tips

Check the moon at the same time each evening for a week before switching times — the shape changes are clearest on a fixed schedule. A torch-and-ball session answers the shape question better than words. Missing-moon nights go in the diary too: hiding is part of the pattern.

This lesson pairs with the Moon flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Science, Nature & Discovery (Class 31).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SCIENCE, NATURE & DISCOVERY · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Day and Night — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson answers the classic bedtime question — where does the sun GO at night? — with the biggest idea in the set: the sun goes nowhere. Earth spins, and your side turning away from the light is what night is. A torch and a ball make it visible.

What is this?

Day and night come from Earth spinning like a top: one full turn takes 24 hours, and that turn is what a day means. The side of Earth facing the sun has day; the side turned away has night. We are riding the spin, so the light sweeps past us every 24 hours.

What does it mean?

The sun does not rise or set — it shines steadily while the ground under your feet turns. Sunrise is your spot on Earth rotating into the light; sunset is it rotating out. And bedtime here is playtime on the far side of the world, where children are facing the sun.

What does the child need to know?

Earth turns once every 24 hours — that is what a day is. The spin never stops; nobody feels it because everything turns together. When your child goes to bed, families on the opposite half of the planet are sitting down to breakfast in their daytime.

Why this matters

This is the set’s biggest scale-up: from a garden to a spinning planet. The torch-on-a-ball model makes the invisible rotation visible and answers the night question with mechanics instead of magic — and it quietly explains time zones before bedtime.

What it teaches

Model thinking (ball as Earth, torch as sun), the swap-perspective idea (day here, morning over there), scale — from bedroom to planet — and the deep fact that a day is not the sun’s doing but the ground’s turning.

Words to learn

daynightEarthspinsuntorch

Say this to your child

“"The sun does not go anywhere at night — the Earth turns! Our whole planet spins like a top, one turn every day. When our side faces the sun, it is day. As we turn away, night rolls in — and on the far side of the world, children are waking up to their morning. We are all riding the same spinning ball."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: what two scenes can you find — a sunny day side and a starry night side? The child is standing right between them.
  2. Ask the bedtime question: where does the sun go at night? Collect the guesses, then flip it: the sun stays put — WE turn away.
  3. Build the model: torch on, ball out. The lit half is having day, the dark half night. Now give the ball a slow turn — day sweeps across it.
  4. Spin the child: one slow full turn — that took a whole day’s worth. Earth does that in exactly 24 hours, every day, without stopping.
  5. Try the other side: when it is bedtime here, children on the far side of the world are heading out to play in their morning sun. Same sun, different turn of the ball.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: what two scenes can you find in the picture? Which side is day and which is night? Can you find the stars? What is on the sunny half of the picture?

Ask your child

"What is Earth doing right now — standing still or spinning?" "How long does one full spin take?" "Where does the sun go at night?" "When it is bedtime here, what are children on the far side doing?"

What your child can say or do

"WE are the ones spinning — not the sun!" "One turn equals one whole day!" Your child may spin slowly on the spot announcing sunset and sunrise, hold a torch over a globe at bedtime, or wave goodnight to the children whose morning is starting on the far side of the world.

Out in the real world

The spin shows up daily: the sun’s arc across the sky, shadows swinging round the garden, breakfast-afternoon-bedtime in a steady loop. When a faraway cousin sends a breakfast photo at your bedtime, your child has the answer ready: the ball keeps turning.

Try it together

Planet spin game: your child is Earth, a torch-wielding grown-up is the sun. Face the torch — "day!" — turn slowly away — "night!" — one full turn, "a whole day!" Then swap roles and let them call the light. Add a toy animal on their shoulder: does the animal see the sun all day?

Understanding check

Ask: "What makes day and night? How long is one spin? Where does the sun go at night?" Earth’s turning, 24 hours, nowhere — we turn away = landed.

Parent tips

Dim the room for the torch model — the lit half is much clearer. Let your child find the exact spot where their own bedroom sits on the ball and predict its light. The far-side fact lands best with a real map: pick a country, check its bedtime, wonder together.

This lesson pairs with the Day and Night flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Science, Nature & Discovery (Class 31).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SCIENCE, NATURE & DISCOVERY · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Volcano — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson lets your child run an eruption — a safe one — while learning the honest version: deep underground, rock melts, pressure builds, and mountains occasionally let go. The kitchen model bubbles; the real thing creeps downhill glowing, and both are Earth showing its hot inside.

What is this?

A volcano is a mountain connected to the hot rock deep below the ground. Down there it gets so hot that rock melts; the melted rock — lava — rises, pressure builds, and sometimes the mountain erupts, pouring glowing lava down its sides until it cools hard into new rock.

What does it mean?

The ground under your feet has a hot heart: the deeper you go, the hotter it gets, and volcanoes are the places where that heat sometimes reaches the top. Lava is rock so hot it flows — and when it cools, it is rock again. The kitchen model copies the flow, not the heat.

What does the child need to know?

Real lava is over a thousand degrees and creeps downhill slowly, like extremely thick honey — slow enough that people can usually walk away from it. There are about 1,500 active volcanoes on Earth, and most grumble gently, puffing steam instead of booming. Erupted lava hardens into brand-new rock.

Why this matters

Volcanoes show Earth as active — the ground has an inside, and it is hot. Running the baking-soda model gives your child the predict-pour-watch thrill of experiments, and the honest comparison (foam versus lava) keeps it real without a single nightmare.

What it teaches

Cause-and-effect under pressure (build-up, eruption, flow), model-versus-reality comparison, the underground-heat idea, and experimental thrills with grown-up handles on anything hot — a first lab-safety division of labour.

Words to learn

volcanolavaerupthotrockpressure

Say this to your child

“"A volcano is a mountain with a job: when the rock deep underground melts and the pressure builds up, the mountain erupts and glowing lava pours down its sides. It creeps slowly, like the thickest honey ever — and when it cools down, it turns back into solid rock. Our kitchen volcano does the same flow with bubbles: the grown-up handles the fizz, you handle the watching."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: what is the mountain doing, and what color is the lava? Is the child watching from far away or close up? Name the eruption.
  2. Tell the inside story: deep underground, rock melts because of the heat; the melted rock is called lava, and it climbs and climbs until the mountain lets go.
  3. Compare flows: real lava creeps like extremely thick honey, glowing red-hot, and cools into new rock. Where do you think our foam model will flow?
  4. Run the kitchen eruption: build a dough mountain around a cup, spoon in baking soda, and let the grown-up pour the vinegar — then step back and watch it bubble over.
  5. Close the loop: our foam lava flowed downhill just like the real thing — but the real lava is rock a thousand degrees hot, which is why a grown-up handles all heat, always.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: what is the mountain doing? What color is the lava pouring down? Is the child standing close or far away? Where do you think the lava will stop?

Ask your child

"What is lava — melted what?" "Why does a volcano erupt?" "What happens to lava when it cools down?" "Who pours the vinegar in our kitchen volcano — and why?"

What your child can say or do

"Lava is rock that melted!" "It cools back into rock — new rock!" Your child may rebuild the dough volcano daily, narrate eruptions with a slow honey-voice, or explain that volcanoes are "mountains letting off steam — and sometimes lava".

Out in the real world

Volcano evidence is in the ground everywhere: black rocky cliffs in holiday photos, hot springs and steaming vents in volcanic countries, and the island chain of Hawaii — whole islands built by cooled lava, layer on layer, still growing today.

Try it together

Dough volcano repeat lab: build the mountain, erupt, then reshape and re-run — does more baking soda make a bigger flow? Steeper mountain, faster foam? Let your child change ONE thing each round, exactly like a fair test, and crown the best eruption of the day.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is lava? What happens when it cools? Who handles the hot parts of experiments?" Melted rock, it hardens into new rock, grown-ups = landed.

Parent tips

Film the eruption on the second run — after the surprise, your child will want to watch the foam flow frame by frame. Old dough mountains dry into permanent volcanoes for the toy shelf. Book the science-fair volcano for later; yours already works.

Staying safe

The kitchen eruption is fizz, not fire — but the honest rule stands: grown-ups handle anything hot, and real lava at over a thousand degrees is a look-at-pictures, never-go-near event. On holiday near volcanic areas, marked paths and barrier fences are there because the ground itself can be hot; feet stay on the safe side, always.

This lesson pairs with the Volcano flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Science, Nature & Discovery (Class 31).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SCIENCE, NATURE & DISCOVERY · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Dinosaur Fossil — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson solves a mystery your child may not have noticed yet: nobody alive has ever seen a dinosaur — so how do we know them? Buried bones, pressed to stone, dug out slowly. The cookie excavation lets your child dig like a real palaeontologist, and slow hands win.

What is this?

A fossil is the stone-hard remains of a living thing from long ago. An animal buried quickly by mud or sand skips the rotting; over millions of years, pressure turns the buried bones to rock. Dig them up, and the skeleton tells you everything.

What does it mean?

Fossils are evidence, the only witnesses left: no photos, no videos, just buried clues. Scientists who read them — palaeontologists — are detectives, working out what dinosaurs ate, how big they grew and how they moved, one brush-stroke at a time.

What does the child need to know?

A fossil needs fast burial: mud or flood sand must cover the bones before they can rot, and then age plus deep pressure slowly turn them to stone. The digging is famously slow — one real bone can take weeks, brushed free grain by grain. Museums are full of the results.

Why this matters

Fossils introduce deep time — millions of years — in the gentlest way, and they frame scientists as clue-readers, which is exactly the habit your child is building. The cookie dig trains the patience: real discoveries come from careful hands, not fast ones.

What it teaches

Evidence-based thinking (how we know what nobody saw), fine motor control in the excavation, patience with a slow process, and vocabulary — fossil, palaeontologist, excavation — that makes museum visits into homecomings.

Words to learn

fossilbonesdigburiedstoneclues

Say this to your child

“"Nobody has ever seen a living dinosaur — but we know them anyway, because of fossils. When a dinosaur died and got buried quickly by mud, its bones stayed put for millions of years while the pressing turned them to stone. Scientists dig them out with tiny brushes, so slowly that one bone can take weeks. The bones are the story."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: what is the child brushing dirt off? Can you find the dinosaur’s ribs, its leg, its skull? Name the buried skeleton.
  2. Ask the mystery question: nobody alive ever saw a dinosaur — so how do we know what they looked like? The buried bones tell us.
  3. Explain the making: a dinosaur must be buried fast — under mud or flood sand — before it has time to rot; then years beyond counting press the bones slowly into stone.
  4. Set the cookie dig: treat the chocolate chips as buried fossils and the cookie as the rock around them. Dig out every chip whole with a toothpick — slow hands win, exactly like a real dig.
  5. Read the findings: lay your excavated "fossils" in a row. What kind of creature left them? That is palaeontology — reading stories told in stone.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: what is the child brushing? What is hiding under the dirt? Can you find the bones — where is the skull, where is a leg? Is the child brushing fast or slowly?

Ask your child

"What is a fossil?" "How do we know about dinosaurs if nobody saw them?" "Why must bones be buried quickly?" "What does a palaeontologist do all day?"

What your child can say or do

"Fossils are bones turned to STONE!" "Slow hands win — like a real palaeontologist!" Your child may brush every flowerbed carefully on the lookout for buried clues, lay toys in mud "for the future to find", or explain that museums are full of "stone bones".

Out in the real world

Fossils sit in plain reach: ammonite shapes in beach stones, fossil-hunting beaches with chalk cliffs, museum halls where a real T. rex skull leans over the rail. Even a garden pebble with a shell print is a fossil clue — the past, pressing into the present.

Try it together

Cookie excavation dig site: one chocolate-chip cookie, one toothpick, one small brush per palaeontologist. Rule of the site: every chip out whole, no crumbling the "rock". Then record the find — draw the chips in a grid, like a real dig map. Repeat until the site is exhausted and the palaeontologist is snack-full.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is a fossil? How did the bones turn to stone? Who digs them up slowly?" Stone-hard old bones, pressing for ages, palaeontologists = landed.

Parent tips

The toothpick-and-brush combo matters — the brush does the final cleaning, just like real digs, and the two tools slow the digging to science speed. If a natural history museum is within reach, go within a fortnight: your child will walk in naming the palaeontologist’s job out loud.

This lesson pairs with the Dinosaur Fossil flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Science, Nature & Discovery (Class 31).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SCIENCE, NATURE & DISCOVERY · AGES 4–5 YEARS

What Magnets Attract — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson is the perfect first experiment: a magnet, ten household objects, and one question — will it stick? Your child predicts, tests and sorts, and discovers that "metal" is not the answer: only iron and steel stick, and the surprises are the lesson.

What is this?

Magnets pull — but only on certain things. Iron and steel hold fast; wood, plastic, glass, paper and fabric stay stubborn. Many everyday "metal" objects — most coins, foil and drink cans — are metals a magnet ignores. The magnet is the only honest judge.

What does it mean?

Not all metal is magnetic: the pull works on iron and steel, which is why the fridge door holds a drawing and the aluminium can does not. Sorting stick from no-stick is classification, and the magnet does the sorting instantly — no opinions needed.

What does the child need to know?

A magnet always sticks to iron and steel — spoons, keys, radiators, the fridge door. It never sticks to wood, plastic, glass, paper or cloth, no matter how hard you wish. Foil and most coins fail the test: they are metals, just not the magnetic kind.

Why this matters

This is the full predict-test-conclude cycle in one safe game: your child guesses before touching, tests with the magnet, and sorts results into piles. Being wrong out loud — the spoon stuck, the coin did not — is exactly how experiments teach.

What it teaches

Prediction before testing (the scientist’s core habit), sorting into two clean categories, vocabulary for materials (iron, steel, plastic, wood, metal), and the surprise-mindset: wrong guesses are findings, not failures.

Words to learn

magnetstickmetalsteeltestsort

Say this to your child

“"A magnet is a picky puller — it only sticks to iron and steel. Wooden spoons? No. Plastic bricks? No. The metal zip? Sometimes yes! Before we test, we guess — that is what scientists do. Then the magnet tells the truth, and into the piles it goes: STICKS, and no."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: what is in the child’s hand, and what shape does it have? Can you count the paperclips waiting nearby? Name the tool — a horseshoe magnet.
  2. Set the game: guess FIRST, test SECOND. Will the spoon stick? The coin? The toy car? Call every guess out loud before the magnet touches anything.
  3. Run the house hunt: ten objects, one magnet — spoons, coins, keys, toys, zips — even the door handle. Stick or no?
  4. Sort the verdicts: two piles on the table — STICKS on the left, NO on the right. What did the stickers share? Iron and steel, mostly hiding inside things.
  5. Land the surprise: coins and foil are metal but do NOT stick — not all metal is magnetic. The magnet is the only judge that never gets it wrong.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: what is the child holding? What shape is the magnet? Can you find all the paperclips — how many are there? Do you think they will all stick?

Ask your child

"Does a magnet stick to wood?" "What kinds of metal do magnets pull?" "What do we do first — guess or test?" "What did the coin do when we tested it?"

What your child can say or do

"The coin did NOT stick — but the spoon did!" "Guess first, then the magnet tells the truth!" Your child may test every fridge door in the house, walk the kitchen with a magnet like a metal detector, or announce "not all metal sticks!" at unrelated moments for weeks.

Out in the real world

Stick tests are everywhere once the magnet is out: the radiator (sticks), the mirror frame (often not), zip pulls, bath toys, the cutlery drawer. The fridge door becomes a daily test station — and gift shops sell magnet sets that keep the hunt going for years.

Try it together

Mystery-bag magnetism: fill a cloth bag with safe household objects — some steel, some not. Your child predicts what is inside, then fishes with a magnet through the fabric: sticks means steel, no means mystery unsolved — pull it out and check. Sorting, predicting, surprise: the full loop.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do magnets stick to? Do all metals stick? What comes first — the guess or the test?" Iron and steel, no, the guess = landed.

Parent tips

Let your child keep the two sorted piles for a day and re-test anything that objects to its verdict — re-testing is real science. Fridge-magnet letters make a bonus round: they stick because their backs hide soft iron.

Staying safe

Small magnets and small parts are a baby-sibling hazard: swallowed magnets can pinch inside the body and cause real harm, so magnet play happens up high, out of baby territory, and every magnet gets counted back at the end. Big snap-together magnets also pinch fingers hard — little hands use big magnets, gently.

This lesson pairs with the What Magnets Attract flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Science, Nature & Discovery (Class 31).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SCIENCE, NATURE & DISCOVERY · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Magnet Force — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson goes one step past what sticks: force with no contact at all. Your child feels the invisible pull when two magnets meet, the invisible cushion when they argue, and the strangest trick of all — a paperclip lifting while paper stands in between.

What is this?

A magnet can move things without touching them: it pulls steel from across a gap, and it grips hardest at its two ends — the poles. Turn two magnets the wrong way round and they push apart, no hands needed. The force even works through paper, water and a table top.

What does it mean?

Force at a distance is the wild part: nothing is touching, yet something moves. Every magnet has a north and a south pole, and the rule is absolute — opposite poles pull together, matching poles push apart. The invisible cushion your child feels in their palm is a push they can trust.

What does the child need to know?

Both ends of a magnet are poles — north and south. Opposite poles grab each other; matching poles shove apart. No exceptions, ever. Magnetic force reaches through paper, wood, water and skin, but it fades fast: twice as far away means much less pull.

Why this matters

Feeling a push with no visible cause stretches the invisible-things-are-real idea from wind to a new level — force without contact. It also hands your child a rule with no exceptions (opposites pull, matches push) and the joy of a power they can hold in one hand.

What it teaches

Feeling invisible forces directly (pull, push, through-things), rule-testing (flip the magnet, check the rule), vocabulary — poles, attract, repel — and early physics wonder: this same invisible-force idea grows up into gravity and electricity.

Words to learn

pullpushpolesforceattractdistance

Say this to your child

“"A magnet moves things with no touching at all — that is its superpower. It grips hardest at its two ends, the poles. Turn two magnets so opposite poles meet and they grab each other. Flip one around and they push apart — you can feel the invisible cushion! And the force works through paper and even water. Try it: nothing touches, and things still move."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: what is hanging under the magnet, and what is the child lifting with no hands? Name the trick — force with no fingers.
  2. Feel the pull: hold two magnets loosely, ends toward each other — let them snap together and feel the grab. That force crossed the gap with no touching.
  3. Feel the push: flip one magnet and try again — the same ends shove apart like an invisible cushion. Opposite poles pull, matching poles push. Always.
  4. Break the barrier: slip a sheet of paper between the two — the clip still lifts! The force goes through things. Try a table top, a book, a cup of water.
  5. Map the poles: name the two ends north and south, test all four combinations, and let your child announce the rule like a law of nature — because it is one.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: what is hanging from the magnet? Is the magnet holding the paperclip from above? What colors can you find on the magnet? What is the child lifting without fingers?

Ask your child

"What are the two ends of a magnet called?" "What do opposite poles do — pull or push?" "Can magnet force work through paper?" "What did you feel when two matching poles met?"

What your child can say or do

"Opposites attract — matching poles push apart!" "I felt the invisible cushion — it pushed my hand away!" Your child may float magnets across the table like a duel, test whether the force works through their sleeve, or explain that poles "are the strongest bits of the magnet".

Out in the real world

Magnetic force is at work all over the house: the fridge seal that clicks shut, cabinet latches, the magnetic clasp on a bag, phone cases that snap on. Train sets and magnetic tiles run on the same poles rule your child just felt in the palm of a hand.

Try it together

Magnet maze: draw a maze on card, lay a paperclip "racer" on top, and steer it through from below with a bar magnet — no touching the racer, force through the card only. Then race: two racers, two magnets, first to the finish without lifting the magnet. Steady poles win.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do opposite poles do? What do matching poles do? Can the force work through paper?" Pull together, push apart, yes — through things = landed.

Parent tips

The maze needs a roomy paperclip and slow hands — steer from below, wrists low. For the water trick, drop a steel spoon into a cup and run the magnet up the outside: the spoon follows through the wall. Matching-pole pushes deserve a rerun whenever the mood strikes; the invisible cushion never gets old.

Staying safe

Strong magnets are a small-parts danger for baby siblings: if two are swallowed they can pinch tissue inside the body and cause serious harm — magnet play stays up high, and every piece is counted back in. Big snap-together magnets also pinch fingers viciously; little hands use big magnets, slowly.

This lesson pairs with the Magnet Force flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Science, Nature & Discovery (Class 31).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SCIENCE, NATURE & DISCOVERY · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Sound — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson makes sound touchable from both ends: the shaking that makes it — visible as rice dancing on a drum skin — and the shaking that hears it, felt as a buzz in your own throat. Quiet and loud, deep and squeaky, all come down to one wobbling idea.

What is this?

Every sound starts with a shake: a drum skin wobbles, the shake rides waves through the air to your ear, and the last wobble lands on your eardrum — which wobbles too. That final wobble is hearing. No shaking, no sound.

What does it mean?

Sound is movement you can see and feel, not just hear: rice jumps on a drum, your throat buzzes when you hum, a big slow wobble sounds deep and a fast one sounds squeaky. Quiet means small shakes; loud means big ones — volume is shaking size.

What does the child need to know?

Bigger things wobble slower, and slow wobbles sound deep — that is why a big drum booms while a small one taps. Sound can travel through your bones too: tuck your fingertips lightly over your ears and say something, and your own voice arrives loud and clear from the inside.

Why this matters

Sound turns an invisible everyday thing into a testable one: your child can see the rice jump, feel the throat buzz, and hear the difference a size makes. It also explains the volume knob, the quiet game, and why libraries whisper — all one wobbling idea.

What it teaches

Multisensory evidence (seeing, feeling, hearing the same shake), cause-and-effect with size and pitch, impulse control through quiet-loud games, and the body knowledge that your own throat and ears are vibration equipment.

Words to learn

soundvibrationdrumloudquietwobble

Say this to your child

“"Every sound starts as a wobble — a shake! The drum skin shakes, the shake rides the air all the way to your ear, and your eardrum shakes back: that is hearing. Put your fingers on your throat and hum — feel it? You are making a wobble right now. Big slow wobbles boom, tiny fast ones squeak."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: what is the child playing, and what is rippling out from the drum? Name it — sound waves, made by shaking.
  2. Feel it first: fingers on the throat, hum like a bee. That buzz is the vibration — you ARE the sound machine.
  3. Make it visible: stretch a balloon skin tight over a bowl, dust it with dry rice, and tap a metal pot loudly next to it. Every boom, the rice jumps — the shake, made seeable.
  4. Sort the sizes: big drum, slow deep wobble — boom. Small drum, fast tiny wobble — tap. Loud is a big shake, quiet is a small one.
  5. Travel the sound: tuck fingertips over your ears and talk — the sound sneaks through your own bones. Then whisper: how small can a wobble get?

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: what is the child playing? What is rippling out from the drum? Can you pretend to tap a drum? Does the sound look like it is going far away or staying close?

Ask your child

"What is every sound made of?" "What did the rice do when the drum boomed?" "Why does a big drum sound deep?" "How can you hear a sound with your fingers over your ears?"

What your child can say or do

"Sound is a wobble that your ear catches!" "The rice is jumping — I can SEE the sound!" Your child may hum with fingers on throat to prove the buzz, tap pots gently near the rice drum to make it dance, or whisper "small wobble" instead of quiet.

Out in the real world

Sound shakes are everywhere: a speaker’s cone you can feel humming, a window buzzing when a lorry passes, the purr of a cat against your hand. The volume game works in every room — big shakes for the playground, small shakes for the library, and now your child knows why.

Try it together

Rice-drum rock band: one bowl with a balloon-skin or cling-film top, rice sprinkled, and a pot-and-spoon kit for drums. Play loud beside it and watch the rice mosh, then tiptoe the taps — barely a grain moves. Chart it: boom, jump; whisper, still. Sound, sized.

Understanding check

Ask: "What makes every sound? What does loud mean for the shaking? What did the rice show us?" Wobbling, big shakes, the vibration = landed.

Parent tips

Balloon skins beat cling film for bounce — stretch tight and tape well. Keep the rice on the drum, not the floor, with a tray underneath. The ears-and-speak trick is a reliable wow: your child’s own voice, arriving through bone. Follow with a quiet walk and a hunt for the smallest wobbles they can hear.

This lesson pairs with the Sound flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Science, Nature & Discovery (Class 31).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SCIENCE, NATURE & DISCOVERY · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Shadow — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson turns a puddle of dark on the pavement into light physics: your child’s body stops the sunshine, and the shape of the stopping follows them all day — long at breakfast, short at noon, gone after dark, and reborn behind a torch for puppet shows.

What is this?

A shadow is the dark shape made where something blocks light: your body stops the sunshine on its way to the ground, and the dark patch that results is shaped exactly like the stopping — you. Move, and the shadow moves; more light or less light, and it stretches or shrinks.

What does it mean?

Light travels in straight lines, and it cannot go through you — so behind you there is a light-shaped hole in the daylight. Shadows are always on the side away from the light: sun in front, shadow behind. No light, no shadow — a cloudy night makes none at all.

What does the child need to know?

Your shadow runs longest when the sun hangs low in the sky — breakfast time, supper time — and shrinks to almost nothing at midday, when it crouches right under your feet. Shadow puppets work because the torch beam is a straight line: block it with a hand, and the wall shows the hand’s shape, huge.

Why this matters

Shadows are physics your child can make with their own body, chase on any sunny day, and command behind a torch. The changing length teaches that the sun moves across the sky — or really, that we turn — and shadow play turns blocking light into theatre.

What it teaches

Observation over a whole day (long, short, gone), positional reasoning (shadow always points away from the light), creative hand-eye play in puppet form, and the seed of the day-and-night lesson: light, blocked and moving.

Words to learn

shadowlightsuntorchblockshape

Say this to your child

“"Your shadow is the dark shape where your body stops the light. The sunshine cannot go through you, so it lands behind you as a you-shaped patch. In the morning it stretches long, at noon it hides short under your feet, and at night — no sun, no shadow. But a torch will build you a new one any time you want."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: where is the child standing, and can you find the shadow? Is it long or short? Name it — the shape of the light being stopped.
  2. Explain the making: light travels in straight lines and cannot pass through your body, so behind you lands a dark patch shaped exactly like the blocker — you.
  3. Chase it outside: morning shadow stretches long, noon shadow tucks short underfoot. Draw a chalk line and measure your shadow at both ends of the day.
  4. Ask the direction rule: where does the sun stand? Your shadow points the other way — always away from the light.
  5. Stage the puppet show: darkish room, torch on the wall, hands making birds and dogs. Block the beam, and the wall plays back your shape — bigger than you are.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: where is the child standing? Can you find the child’s shadow? Is the shadow long or short? Which way is the shadow pointing — toward the sun, or away from it?

Ask your child

"What makes a shadow?" "When is your shadow longest — morning or noon?" "Which way does a shadow point?" "What do you need for a shadow puppet show after dark?"

What your child can say or do

"My shadow is me, blocking the light!" "At noon it hides under my feet!" Your child may jump to see if the shadow jumps (it does), measure shadows in chalk all summer, or put on a nightly hand-puppet show that begins the moment the torch comes out.

Out in the real world

Shadows mark the day without a clock: the long breakfast shadow, the vanishing noon one, the stretched evening giant. Watch out for the reversible surprise — a cloudy day has no shadow, but any lamp, phone torch or streetlight will build one on demand, indoors or out.

Try it together

Shadow theatre: a bedsheet screen, a bright torch behind it, and hand puppets — bird (thumbs hooked, fingers flapping), dog (thumb ears), rabbit (two-finger ears). Let your child direct the show, then swap: their hands become the actors. Move the torch closer — the animals grow. Why?

Understanding check

Ask: "What makes a shadow? Which way does it point? When is it longest?" Blocked light, away from the light, low-sun morning and evening = landed.

Parent tips

The chalk-line shadow clock is the two-day project that keeps giving: trace the same spot’s shadow at morning, noon and evening, then repeat next season. Torch puppets need one dim room and one bright beam — and a patient audience of toys. Shadows point away from the light: test it with two lamps and a toy.

This lesson pairs with the Shadow flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Science, Nature & Discovery (Class 31).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SCIENCE, NATURE & DISCOVERY · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Feather — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson answers two bird questions with one object: how do birds fly, and how do they stay warm? Your child races a feather against a stone, watches the air catch every strand, and looks close enough to find the tiny hooks that zip a bird’s coat shut.

What is this?

Feathers are a bird’s built-in gear: long flight feathers catch the air for flying, and soft fluffy down feathers trap warm air close to the body like a duvet. A bird can have thousands of them, zipped neat with its beak.

What does it mean?

The feather wins the drop race because the air catches it: light, wide and spread into strands, it falls slow — while the stone drops straight through. Down works the same trick for warmth: feathers trap air, and trapped air is the best blanket there is.

What does the child need to know?

Birds preen — zipping their feathers tidy with their beaks, like combing a coat. Flight feathers are built from a hollow stem with strands branching off, and those strands hold tiny hooks that clip together. Your winter jacket and sleeping bag copy the fluffiest feathers, strand for strand.

Why this matters

The feather-versus-stone race is a fair test your child can run off any park bench — and the answer (air catches it) links feathers to flying. Finding hooks on a real feather shows that gear can be tiny, and the jacket connection brings bird science to the coat rack.

What it teaches

Fair testing (same height, drop together), cause-and-effect with air resistance at playground scale, close observation with a magnifier, and the design idea: birds and coat makers solved the same problem the same way.

Words to learn

featherbirdflywarmdownair

Say this to your child

“"A feather does two jobs for a bird: the long ones catch the air for flying, and the fluffy ones hold warm air like a duvet. Watch — drop a feather and the air catches it, strand by strand, so it floats down slow. The stone has no such trick; it just drops. And your winter coat? It copies the fluffy kind."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: what is the child holding — soft or scratchy? What color is the feather? Name its two jobs: flying and warm-keeping.
  2. Run the drop race: feather against a small stone, released together from the same height. Which floats, which thuds? The air grabs every feather strand.
  3. Explain the flying: wide flight feathers push against the air like oars — a bird flaps, catches air, and stays up. Stone could never.
  4. Tell the warm secret: under the flight feathers sits fluffy down that traps warm air — your winter jacket is stuffed with the same idea.
  5. Look close on a real feather: smooth vane on one side, fluffy on the other, and along the strands — tiny hooks that zip the whole thing shut.

Look closer at the picture

Ask your child: what is the child holding? Is the feather soft or hard? What color is it? Who do you think the feather belonged to?

Ask your child

"What are a bird’s two kinds of feathers for?" "Why does a feather fall slower than a stone?" "What do birds do with their beaks to keep feathers neat?" "What does your winter coat copy from birds?"

What your child can say or do

"The air catches the feather — that is why it floats!" "My coat has down — bird stuff, copied!" Your child may drop leaves, scarves and paper alongside stones all week, preen their own hair in front of the mirror like a bird, or inspect every found feather for hooks.

Out in the real world

Feather signs are everywhere: the pigeon feather by the bus stop, the duvet on your child’s bed, the duck shaking water off its back — water rolls off because preened feathers are zipped tight. The park is a feather showroom; the coat rack is the copycat aisle.

Try it together

Feather-versus-anything Olympics: race a feather against a coin, a leaf, a scarf square and a crumpled paper ball — same height, drop on the count of three. Rank the floaters, then untie the mystery: wide and light floats, small and heavy drops. The air is the judge.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do feathers do for birds? Why does a feather float down slowly? What is your winter coat stuffed with?" Fly and warm, the air catches it, down = landed.

Parent tips

Found feathers get a gentle wash-and-dry before close looking — and a magnifier turns the hooks from a claim into a sighting. Shop feathers work for the race too, but a real one shows the zip. If a bird lets you watch it preen, you have seen the whole lesson in ten seconds.

This lesson pairs with the Feather flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Science, Nature & Discovery (Class 31).
